Mir Raza murder case: Karachi police surgeon among 4 told to appear before judicial commission tomorrow. KARACHI: A judicial commission on Monday summoned the Karachi police surgeon and another member included in the medical board that oversaw the exhumation of Mir Raza Ali’s body — which was found with a gunshot wound in July in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar — at the next hearing. The murder case has been mired in conspiracy, with the 25-year-old victim’s family accusing police of trying to bury the facts and law enforcers initially trying to build the case around the possibility of suicide. Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiyya Syed had previously also pointed out flaws in the findings of Ali’s first autopsy, following which his body was exhumed and a second post-mortem was conducted, whose findings ruled out the possibility of suicide. A one-member judicial commission headed by Sindh High Court Justice Omar Sial, formed to investigate the circumstances and possible negligence in the case, has been holding hearings on the matter. According to the commission’s order issued after today’s hearing, Ferozabad Station House Officer (SHO) Adeel Afzal and Gulistan-i-Jauhar police station Head Moharir Zeeshan have also been asked to appear before the commission at the next hearing on Sept 8. SHO Afzal is deployed at the Ferozabad police station, where the case was initially registered under charges of kidnapping following Ali’s disappearance on July 28. His body was found a day later, and following Ali’s second autopsy, the probe was transferred to the Zaman Town police station in August, with murder charges added to the FIR. Head Moharir Zeeshan is among those who visited the crime scene after Ali’s body was found. In the order, Justice Sial stated that he had “realised during this hearing that the initial witnesses’ statements have not been provided to me. I have drawn an adverse inference from this”. He recalled that on the first hearing held by the commission, the Sindh police was directed to provide the statements of all witnesses recorded under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. “However, this has not been done,” Justice Sial noted. He added that a notice was issued to Sindh Deputy Inspector General (Crime and Investigation) Amir Farooqui — who also heads the new police team formed to probe the case — after which two statements from Ali’s friends, Abdul Razique and Muhammad Hasem, recorded on August 1, were provided by the Sindh Police. “They say that there is no other document missing from the record after the submission of these two statements. The notice to DIG Amir Farooqui is therefore withdrawn on the assurance of the Home additional secretary that no further documents are missing,” the order read. The additional secretary was also instructed to probe whether there were forensic, ballistic and chemical reports which had not been provided to the commission, and if there were any such reports, their copies should be submitted in a sealed envelope. The case Days after the recovery of Ali’s body on July 29, Dr Syed had told Geo News that the post-mortem findings in the case had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. On August 6, a Karachi court took up an application by Ali’s father, allowed the exhumation of his body, ordered the formation of a medico-legal board for the purpose and directed that a second autopsy of Ali’s body be conducted. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with police surgeon Dr Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed. But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, the counsel for Ali’s family, Nasir, accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts. The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on August 8. A day later, the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death while Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town police station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered. The order for the probe team’s reconstitution also showed that a murder charge had been added to the first information report. The same day, the Sindh government decided to seek a judicial commission for the case’s investigation, only to defer the plan a day later after Ali’s family said they had made no such demand and had faith in the new investigation team. On Aug 19, Ali’s parents, Mir Hussain and Mariam Hussain, wrote to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, seeking his “direct supervision of the murder investigation”. They also urged the chief minister to order an investigation and departmental inquiry into the previous investigation team and immediately suspend the officers involved. The provincial government acknowledged the letter and announced the decision on Aug 23 to form a judicial commission to determine whether the investigation in the case was being conducted impartially and to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ali’s death. However, soon after the announcement, the counsel for Ali’s family raised objections and later approached the Sindh High Court (SHC). The petition was filed on August 24 in objection to the provincial government’s decision to form a judicial commission and sought the formation of an independent and multi-agency JIT “comprising officers who have had no previous involvement in the case” in place of the commission. On Sept 2, the SHC dismissed a petition filed by Ali’s family, seeking the formation of a JIT to probe his murder, observing that constituting such a body was the “prerogative of the government”. Meanwhile, the final report of Ali’s second post-mortem for the Mir Raza Ali murder case confirmed that his death was caused by a gunshot wound to the back. “Death occurred due to cardiac rupture consequent to perforating firearm injury of the chest,” the report stated, adding that the entry wound was on the posterior thorax (back) and the exit wound on the anterior thorax (front of the chest). “The findings are inconsistent with suicide as the manner of death,” it confirmed.

Pakistan rejects India's 'baseless' claims on status of occupied Kashmir. The Foreign Office (FO) on Monday rejected Indian claims about the status of occupied Kashmir, saying that New Delhi’s “unilateral claims of sovereignty have no bearing on the internationally recognised disputed status of the territory”. The statement came after the United Nations voted on Friday to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries aimed at “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses, making their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe. India was among the 164 countries that voted in favour of the resolution. However, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs on Sunday issued a statement , saying that the resolution did not constitute the endorsement of any specific map, projection or depiction of natural boundaries. It also said that its territory, “including Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh”, must be depicted in accordance with its “official map”, adding that any deviation was “unacceptable”. In the statement issued on Monday, FO Spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said: “Pakistan categorically rejects India’s baseless assertions regarding the status of Jammu and Kashmir which are contrary to internationally recognised facts.” “India’s unilateral actions and continued illegal occupation cannot alter the internationally recognised disputed status of Jammu and Kashmir,” he said. He added that the Kashmir issue remained one of the oldest unresolved internationally recognised disputes on the agenda of the United Nations (UN) Security Council. “The relevant UN resolutions stipulate that its final disposition must be made in accordance with the relevant Security Council resolutions and the will of the Kashmiri people, expressed through a free and impartial plebiscite under UN auspices,” he added. “The official UN maps, which depict Jammu and Kashmir as a disputed territory, remain the only cartographic representation of its current legal status,” he said. “India’s so-called official maps and unilateral claims of sovereignty have no bearing on the status of the disputed territory,” the FO spokesperson said. “Pakistan urged the international community to ensure that India immediately stops human rights violations in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir, and fulfils its commitment towards the realisation of the right to self-determination of the Kashmiri people, in line with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions,” the FO spokesperson concluded. The UN resolution said the new map, known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection, “is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world”. It urged member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. The United States had slammed the resolution, saying such moves are “the reason this institution is losing its credibility”.

Fatima Sana penalised for Verma send-off in Women’s Asia Cup match against India. Pakistan captain Fatima Sana has been fined 10 per cent of her match fee for breaching the ICC Code of Conduct during the team’s Women’s Asia Cup match against India, according to an International Cricket Council media release published on Monday. The offence occurred in the Women’s Asia Cup clash between India and Pakistan on Saturday, where the skipper dismissed Indian opener Shafali Verma and gestured towards the pavilion as a send-off. As per the media release, this gesturing meant Fatima was found in a Level 1 breach of the governing body’s Code of Conduct, specifically Article 2.5 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel. This offence pertains to “using language, actions or gestures which disparage, or which could provoke an aggressive reaction from a batter upon his/her dismissal during an International Match.” The contest was a heavily one-sided affair, which saw India blow Pakistan out of the water. The Green Shirts were bowled out for 55, their lowest-ever score in T20 internationals, owing to a masterful spin-show by India. The Women in Blue breezed through the chase, hampered only by an early three-wicket haul by the Pakistan skipper, which saw her remove the Indian top order. In addition to the match fees penalty, one demerit point was also added to Fatima’s disciplinary record, bringing her tally to two. Her singular earlier offence for a 24-month period had come in a match against Ireland in Dublin in August 2025. “Fatima admitted the offence and accepted the sanction proposed by Supriya Rani Das of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees, so there was no need for a formal hearing,” said the release, adding that the charge was levelled by the two on-field umpires, the third and the fourth umpires. While Level 1 offences usually incur a “maximum penalty of 50 per cent of a player’s match fee, and one or two demerit points,” an accumulation of four or more demerit points within the stipulated period would entail they get converted to suspension points, with the player getting banned thereby. Pakistan play their next match of the Asia Cup in Dubai against Hong Kong on Monday night, where they will look to seal their semi-final berth.

Karachi police briefly detain protesting family members of Pakistani sailors held hostage by Somali pirates. KARACHI: Some family members of Pakistani sailors, who have been held hostage by Somali pirates aboard the MT Honour 25 for more than four months, were briefly detained on Monday morning while they were staging a sit-in at Karachi’s Sharea Faisal. The MT Honour 25, a Palau-flagged oil tanker, was hijacked by armed pirates off the coast of Puntland, Somalia, on April 21. Besides 10 crew members from Pakistan, the hostages include seamen from Indonesia, India and Sri Lanka. During more than four months of their captivity, no significant progress has been reported either in negotiations or in the payment of the ransom, said to be around $3 million, for their recovery. Their families have staged protests for their recovery multiple times. On Sunday, they began an overnight sit-in at Sharea Faisal outside the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ (Mofa) liaison office and planned to march to the Supreme Court registry on Monday morning. But police reached the protest site before that and detained some of them. They were later released, the wife of one of the hostages confirmed to Dawn in the afternoon. “They were taken to the police station and kept there for a long time, and the police were not allowing us to see them. The police misbehaved with us and told us to go away,” said Ayesha Ameen, whose husband, Ameen Bin Shams, was a fitter on the hijacked ship. “They were arrested around 7:45am,” added Ayesha, who was not detained by police. She said that the protesters were taken to the Tipu Sultan police station and alleged that 11 protesters were detained, including “underage individuals”. A police official, who requested anonymity, also confirmed that the detained individuals had been released. A senior police officer, who wished not to be named, denied that any protester was arrested. He said if there had been an arrest, it would have been mentioned in the police’s roznamcha (logbook). Instead, the officer asserted that the police had engaged the protestors since Sunday night. He said police officers had tried to persuade the families to vacate the place when they gathered at the Mofa office and asked them to hold their protest at a designated venue such as Karachi Press Club. The officer told Dawn that the police dispersed the protesters without using any force. He also denied resorting to baton charges against the demonstrators. Earlier, Ayesha recorded a video message at the protest site and said the families had been demanding the recovery of the hostages for four and a half months; however, “no one is listening to us”. She added that the protesters were not blocking any roads or engaged in illegal activity but were merely protesting peacefully. “We came here for the hostages’ release, not to become prisoners ourselves,” she added. Another protester recorded a video inside a vehicle that appeared to be a police van. Police personnel could be seen standing outside the van in the video, in which Talib Raza, the maternal uncle of a second engineer on the ship, decried the detention of the protesters. “We have been arrested — our women, elders and kids. It is shameful. “Bilawal Bhutto sahib, we did not expect this from you,” Raza said, expressing disappointment. In another video, a woman was also seen inside a vehicle that appeared to be a police van. Meanwhile, another woman could be heard saying, “Look, we are being arrested. This is our government, and this is our police. We are being taken away only because we spoke up for ourselves.” In a video shared by Ayesha, two police officials could be seen manhandling an individual and forcing him into the police mobile. Distress messages Since the sailors’ hijacking, the crew has also made several emotional videos and audio appeals , while reporting that they have run out of clean water, food and medicine. The last message from them came on August 7, more than 100 days after being taken hostage by Somali pirates. In that video, they appealed directly to the Pakistani government for their release. They appeared to be in a state of extreme distress, with most looking sick and weak. The hostages requested that the Pakistani government talk to the Somali pirates and take steps to release them. The hostages are victims of an “ ownership crisis ” because it is not clear who owns the ship, and the man previously thought to be the owner was later revealed to be more likely a middleman who hired them. Last month, in a meeting with the International Maritime Organisation’s head, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar pressed for “urgent and effective institutional intervention” for the return of the Pakistani sailors. Earlier that month, he had also directed “stakeholders” to intensify diplomatic engagement with national and international partners to facilitate the release. The Foreign Office has also maintained that it remains “actively engaged” to secure the release of the seamen. Additional reporting by Imtiaz Ali

Govt decides to urgently address shortage of engineering, technical staff at Pims. ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Monday decided to urgently address the shortage of engineering and technical staff at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) as part of efforts to improve efficiency in the health system following a tragic fire incident that killed 14 infants . The meeting was held after the federal government announced steps to address technical issues and hold those responsible accountable for the fire at the Pims Mother and Child Health Centre. According to the health ministry, Health Minister Mustafa Kamal chaired the meeting, which was attended by senior officials from the ministry, the Pims administration, the Capital Development Authority (CDA) and other relevant departments. During the meeting, officials briefed the minister on the status of the heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) system at Pims’ Mother and Child Health Centre, which was affected by the recent fire. CDA officials said work on the HVAC system had been disrupted because the building had been temporarily closed as part of an investigation into the incident. Kamal directed the health secretary to immediately contact the relevant authorities and finalise a timeline for handing over the affected building so that restoration work could resume without delay. The health minister further said suitable engineers and technical experts from the surplus pool created following the abolition of the Pakistan Public Works Department (PWD) should be utilised to address the shortage at Pims. It was also decided that the health ministry would write to the Ministry of Housing and Works for the deployment of suitable engineers, technical experts and other relevant staff at the hospital. “The strengthening of the technical workforce is necessary to ensure uninterrupted and safe healthcare services for patients and newborns,” Kamal said. IHRA starts assessment of Pims The Islamabad Healthcare Regulatory Authority (IHRA) has begun a comprehensive assessment of the hospital’s facilities and services, according to the health ministry. During a separate meeting, the health minister was also briefed on a visit by IHRA technical experts to Pims as part of an assessment of the hospital’s performance, facilities and services against prescribed standards. “The experts are reviewing clinical, surgical, medical, radiology and administrative departments, with the hospital’s performance being assessed against various indicators,” the health ministry said. The ministry said the IHRA team would prepare recommendations aimed at improving Pims’ functioning, raising service standards and modernising the hospital.

Senate panel passes bill proposing death penalty for perpetrators of acid attacks. ISLAMABAD: The Senate Standing Committee on Interior on Monday passed a series of key criminal law amendments, including a bill proposing the death penalty for acid attacks, as it moved to strengthen protections for vulnerable groups and public safety. Chaired by Senator Faisal Saleem Rehman, the committee considered private members’ bills relating to acid crimes, protection of domestic workers, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) safety, anti-rape legislation and consumer protection. The bills were passed despite opposition from State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry, with PPP lawmakers also voting in favour. The Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill moved by Senator Muhammad Abdul Qadir, seeking to amend Section 336B of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) relating to hurt caused by corrosive substances, was passed in the absence of the mover. Citing “the recent incident of acid attack on a lady doctor in Quetta”, the bill states that despite the 2011 amendment, acid attacks continue to cause lifelong disfigurement and trauma. It proposes the punishment of “death or imprisonment for life or imprisonment of not less than 14 years and a fine of Rs2 million” to serve as a strong deterrent. The committee also unanimously passed the Criminal Laws (Amendment) Bill moved by Senator Sarmad Ali, proposing to criminalise the abuse of domestic workers. The Statement of Objects and Reasons notes that “domestic workers constitute one of the most vulnerable segments of society, often subjected to physical violence, sexual abuse, forced labour, and other forms of mistreatment by employers.” It adds that “existing provisions… do not specifically address the abuse arising from dependency and control inherent in domestic work settings”. The proposed section covers physical violence, sexual harassment, threats, forced labour, wage theft, confiscation of identity documents, denial of food or medical care, and humiliating treatment. The proposed penalties are “imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years and fine which may extend to Rs100,000” and “imprisonment for life and fine which may extend to Rs500,000” if the offence causes serious injury or death. The bill also makes employers liable if abuse is committed by household members, “unless the employer took reasonable steps to prevent such abuse”. Schedule II of the Criminal Procedure Code has also been amended to make the offence non-bailable and triable by a court of session. In a move to address public safety hazards, the committee passed the Criminal Laws (Amendment) Act, moved by Senator Shahadat Awan, to amend Sections 286 and 286A of the PPC to criminalise the unauthorised transfer of LPG into smaller cylinders. Noting that such decanting in residential areas and roadside setups poses severe risks, the bill increases the punishment under Section 286 from six months to two years and the fine from Rs1,000 to Rs100,000. Under Section 286A, imprisonment is increased from two to five years and the fine from Rs10,000 to Rs500,000. The Statement of Objects and Reasons notes that “the decanting of LPG from larger cylinders into smaller domestic cylinders without proper safety measures has become a widespread practice in many parts of Pakistan.” It adds that “these unauthorised decanting operations are often conducted in residential areas, workshops, or roadside setups without adherence to safety standards, posing severe risks to public life and property.” The bill proposes raising the punishment under Section 286 from six months to two years and the fine from Rs1,000 to Rs100,000. Under Section 286A, it proposes increasing the term of imprisonment from two to five years and the fine from Rs10,000 to Rs500,000. “The proposed amendments aim to deter negligent and reckless conduct in the handling of explosive and hazardous substances, ensuring greater public safety and accountability.” The committee also unanimously passed the Criminal Laws (Amendment) Bill, moved by Senator Samina Mumtaz Zehri, proposing to insert a new Section 338CA to make “Wrongful Detention of Dead Body” a punishable offence. The Statement of Objects and Reasons highlights that “there have been numerous reports of private hospitals and clinics detaining the dead bodies of patients until their families settle outstanding medical bills”. It cites examples of hospitals that “demand exorbitant advance deposits, sometimes as high as Rs2m to Rs4m” and “withhold dead bodies even when outstanding dues are as low as Rs100,000.” The statement argues that this “not only causes immense psychological harm to grieving families but also denies the deceased the right to timely burial and dignified last rites, which is a fundamental religious obligation in Islam and other religions.” It adds that “the inviolability of human dignity does not cease upon death.” The new section proposes a punishment of up to two years’ imprisonment and/or a fine of Rs500,000 for a first offence, and up to three years’ imprisonment and/or a fine of Rs1m for a second offence or detention beyond 24 hours. Exceptions are provided for autopsies or police investigations. The offence has been made compoundable by the legal heirs. The Anti-Rape (Investigation and Trial) (Amendment) Bill, moved by Bushra Anjum Butt, was also passed, with the committee observing that legislation aimed at strengthening the legal framework against rape should receive appropriate government support. On the consumer side, the committee passed the Islamabad Consumers Protection (Amendment) Bill, also moved by Senator Zehri, to bring private healthcare under the 1995 Act. The bill targets undisclosed fees, non-itemised billing and demands for advance deposits before emergency treatment, and requires hospitals to publicly display fee schedules and provide itemised bills. The committee expressed serious concern over reports that former parliamentarians were being required to obtain a no-objection certificate (NOC) from the Ministry of Interior for the issuance of official passports and that their validity had been reduced from five years to one year. The minister of state for interior said only the internal approval procedure had been changed. The chairman directed that existing law must not be violated and that official passports be issued with five-year validity in accordance with the law. Further deliberation was deferred. The Ministry of Interior also briefed the committee on concerns regarding the unregulated use of social media by minors, stating that a high-powered committee was working on proposals to regulate its use by children. Last week, a 35-year-old woman suffered burns when a man threw acid on her in Karachi’s Upper Gizri area. Earlier in June, 29-year-old Mahnoor Nasir was seriously injured at the Quetta Civil Hospital when another employee threw acid on her. The attacker, later identified by police as Humayun Shah, was said to have been kil­led in an encounter after law enforcers tra­ced him as he attempted to flee on a bus. Meanwhile, Dr Nasir was shifted to Karachi after receiving initial treatment in Quetta. In August, in a landmark judgement, the Supreme Court declared acid attacks more heinous than homicide , describing them as crimes that condemn victims to a “living death”.

Pakistan at ‘very start’ of Test rebuilding process, says bowling coach Noffke. Pakistan are at the “very start” of rebuilding their Test side, bowling coach Ashley Noffke said on Monday, as the team attempts to move past a tumultuous week that has seen sweeping changes to the squad and a shake-up of its coaching staff. “Every nation has a life cycle, and there’ll be moments where they play really great cricket for long periods and then older players will move out and younger players will come in. And we’re at the very start of that process,” Noffke told reporters at Edgbaston. The contrast with England, who are attempting to complete a 3-0 series sweep after emphatic victories at Headingley and Lord’s, could hardly be starker. While Pakistan have brought in a new interim head coach in Mike Hesson, made wholesale changes to their squad and sent Noffke to England at short notice, the hosts have been able to build on a settled pace attack led by Jofra Archer, who says he is finally enjoying a period of stability after years of injury. Pakistan’s changes have opened the door for young fast bowlers Razaullah and Mohammad Imran Jr, with Noffke viewing their presence in England as part of a longer-term plan rather than simply an emergency response to two defeats. “They’re young guys. They haven’t experienced England conditions and they’re over here to learn and grow,” he said. “I think with any life cycle of any cricket team, you need to take a forward-thinking approach to what we might need in the future. I think other teams have been doing that and it’s now our turn to bring young guys over, make sure they get accustomed to conditions that are different to theirs at home.” Both bowlers offer Pakistan something that has been missing from their attack during the series — pace. Noffke said they were “certainly closer to the 140 mark” than some of the quicks Pakistan had previously used. Imran Jr, a left-armer, and Razaullah, a right-armer with a different action, could also provide variety to an attack that has relied heavily on veteran seamer Mohammad Abbas. “Abbas has obviously bowled amazingly through this series and we need to support him as best we can,” Noffke said. Noffke himself was thrust into the Test set-up at short notice, saying he received a message “at 3am” informing him that management was sending him to England. Asked whether he had been given an explanation for the sweeping changes to the squad, he said: “Not really.” “It’s not my job to be in consultation with where they see who’s in and who’s out. That’s obviously the selection panel,” he said. “As we’ve already asked Mike [Hesson] in previous interviews, he’s only just come into that phase. So, like we said before, it’s unsettling, but it’s about getting on with it, focusing on what’s ahead of us as a Test-playing squad and trying to develop in all areas.” The uncertainty surrounding Pakistan has also been compounded by an internal PCB disciplinary inquiry into the conduct of some players announced on Monday. Noffke said he knew no more about the matter than the media did. “As much as you do. And I can be really honest in that — I don’t know too much,” he said. “I sit outside of that decision-making model above us as coaches.” He said the coaching staff had attempted to keep the players focused on the cricket rather than the developments surrounding them. “There’s obviously a feeling of uncertainty, but they’ve just got back on the job,” Noffke said. “I’ve been really impressed with the level of calmness that they’ve taken over the last couple of days once we’ve given them time to talk.” The Australian said Pakistan’s immediate strategy was straightforward: “good Test cricket”, discipline, bowling in good areas and building long partnerships with the bat. Asked whether Pakistan risked becoming a laughing stock following the events on and off the field and whether the team needed to restore some pride, Noffke said performances were the only meaningful answer. “Well, you only install pride with really good cricket, don’t you?” he said. “There’s no question that we need to develop our game. Our Test game needs to improve. But that doesn’t mean that we should be worried about that.” England, meanwhile, are preparing for the possibility of completing a clean sweep with a fast-bowling unit that has been one of the defining features of the series. Archer, who returned to Test cricket in July last year after more than four years away, believes he is now in a “good place” following a succession of career-threatening injuries. The Barbados-born quick arrived in England in 2015 and four years later spearheaded the attack during England’s dramatic World Cup triumph at Lord’s, while also starring in the 2019 Ashes. But an elbow problem subsequently developed, followed by back injuries, and Archer was sidelined from Test cricket from February 2021 until July 2025. The 31-year-old, who continues to play all three international formats, said his long periods away from the game had also brought unexpected benefits. “The time when I was injured, I really got away from cricket,” he told the BBC on Monday. “It’s all been a blur. I didn’t realise how long the time out was, either.” Archer said the enforced breaks allowed him to spend more time at home in Barbados after moving to England. “I got to spend some time at home, because, moving over, I never really got more than a couple of weeks,” he said. “To spend a month here and there, it was really nice.” “I’d be lying if I didn’t say I had a good time away from everything. Now, everything is really nice. My body is in a good place, the team is in a good place and everyone is in a good place. I just want to play cricket.” Archer has played a key role in England’s two victories over Pakistan and will be central to their bid for a 3-0 result at Edgbaston. His presence has also added further weight to an England pace attack featuring Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson, with the group beginning to draw comparisons with England’s celebrated “Fab Four” of Matthew Hoggard, Steve Harmison, Simon Jones and Andrew Flintoff, who helped secure the 2005 Ashes. Pakistan, by contrast, are still deciding whether to field four seamers or retain a spinner, with Noffke saying the decision would depend on the pitch and weather. “We’ve got some really good options now to select in terms of the four seamers, our spinner that can bat. There are some great selection dilemmas, which is nice,” he said. The Edgbaston pitch has plenty of grass, but Noffke expects it to be a good surface. “It looks a good surface. There’s plenty of grass on it, though,” he said. For Pakistan, however, the significance of Wednesday’s Test extends beyond avoiding a series whitewash. With new faces being introduced amid considerable upheaval, Edgbaston could offer an early glimpse of the side Noffke believes is only now beginning the process of rebuilding.

Fire rips through factory in Karachi's Landhi Export Processing Zone, 3 suffer minor injuries. At least three people suffered minor injuries from smoke inhalation after a blaze ripped through a clothing factory in Karachi’s Landhi Export Processing Zone (EPZ) on Monday, Rescue 1122 said. The blaze caused part of the factory to collapse and spread to an adjacent factory, confirmed the Rescue 1122 spokesperson Hassaan Ul Haseeb Khan. However, due to timely evacuation, no loss of life was reported. The fire, which broke out around noon, continued into the night, with more than a dozen fire tenders engaged in extinguishing the blaze. Screengrab from a video shows a fire engulfing a factory in Karachi’s Landhi area on Sept 7, 2026. — Courtesy of Rescue 1122 The spokesperson told Dawn that the control room received a report of a fire at the factory at around 12:53pm. The factory imported used clothes, which were reconditioned and sold in the market. He said a large number of workers were present when the fire broke out, but they managed to evacuate safely on their own. However, when firefighters arrived, seven workers were still trapped inside. Rescue teams subsequently evacuated them safely. “Of them, three became unconscious after inhaling smoke, but they did not sustain any burn injuries and were provided first aid at the scene,” he said. Khan elaborated that the factory comprised a ground floor and three upper storeys and that the entire building was engulfed in flames. “Continued exposure to the fire and heat caused extensive damage to the structure, with around 50 per cent of the building collapsing and the remaining portion sustaining damage.” He added that the intensity of the fire caused it to spread to an adjacent factory whose building was also engulfed in flames, resulting in serious structural damage. The spokesperson said 16 fire tenders from Rescue 1122, the KMC Fire Brigade and the EPZ’s own firefighting setup were engaged in controlling the blaze, which was still raging. The rescue official further said the exact cause of the fire would be ascertained after a proper investigation once the blaze had been brought under control. However, all the goods stored in both factories were destroyed. Screengrab from a video shows a fire engulfing a factory in Karachi’s Landhi area on Sept 7, 2026. — Courtesy of Rescue 1122 Edhi ambulances and volunteers also reached the site to aid in the rescue operation, the Edhi Foundation said. Fires frequently erupt in buildings across Pakistan due to a mix of poor infrastructure, weak enforcement of safety regulations, and widespread negligence. Many structures lack proper fire exits, alarms, and emergency protocols, while faulty wiring and overloaded power systems increase the risk of electrical short circuits. The Gul Plaza inferno , which erupted on the night of January 17 at the mall, claimed at least 73 lives . The blaze took nearly two days to be fully extinguished and left over 1,100 shops in ruins. In early February, a massive fire in a plastic factory at Landhi EPZ had engulfed several nearby factories and took major firefighting efforts to be brought under control after 13 hours. Days later, a fire erupted in a high-rise building near Karachi’s Baloch Colony, with around 150 people evacuated . On February 17, a fire at a chemical factory in the SITE Industrial Area was brought under control. The next month, a blaze that broke out in Imtiaz Superstore’s Zamzama branch was brought under control after hours-long efforts by rescue officials. In June, hundreds of people were evacuated as a fire erupted in the cold storage of a department store situated in a mega shopping mall on Rashid Minhas Road in Federal B Area.

Interpol Pakistan issues 286 red notices in 7 months, 53 fugitives repatriated. ISLAMABAD: Interpol’s National Central Bureau (NCB) in Pakistan issued 286 Red Notices in the last seven months as part of efforts to track fugitives involved in murder, fraud, terrorism and human trafficking, according to Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) Director General Dr Usman Anwar. A Red Notice is a request to law enforcement agencies by Interpol to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender or similar legal action. Anwar, who also heads NCB-Interpol Pakistan, reaffirmed the agency’s resolve on World Day of International Police Cooperation, adding that Islamabad would continue to strengthen collaboration with Interpol and global partners. NCBs serve as each country’s focal point for all Interpol activities. They connect national law enforcement agencies with those in other countries and with the Interpol General Secretariat through a secure global police communications network known as I-24/7, allowing real-time access to databases and services. Anwar said NCB-Interpol Pakistan issued a total of 290 Interpol notices during the period, including two Blue Notices and two Yellow Notices. Yellow Notices are meant to help locate missing persons, often minors, or identify people who are unable to identify themselves, while Blue Notices are issued to collect additional information. Of the 286 Red Notices, 225 were issued for suspects wanted in murder and attempted murder cases, while another 33 were issued for individuals wanted in kidnapping, corruption, robbery and cybercrime cases. The bureau also issued 19 Red Notices for financial fraud and deception, six for human trafficking and three for terrorism. Through international cooperation, 53 fugitives wanted in Pakistan for serious crimes were arrested in different countries and extradited to Pakistan during the same seven-month period. “Today’s crimes are increasingly international. Cybercrime, fugitives and stolen goods driven by organised groups — none of these respect borders,” Anwar told Dawn . “We seek information from other NCBs to help investigations in Pakistan, and we share our criminal data to assist other countries.” He added that NCBs were critical because they could trigger law enforcement action in their respective countries and work directly with counterparts, even between states without diplomatic relations. “When a crime goes beyond our national jurisdiction, we need international support to solve it. Interpol provides that platform,” he stated. According to Interpol’s framework, NCBs contribute national crime data to global databases in accordance with national laws. Red Notices, for example, alert police in all 196 member countries to wanted persons. NCB Pakistan works with domestic law enforcement agencies, other NCBs and sub-bureaus worldwide, as well as the General Secretariat’s offices, to coordinate cross-border investigations, operations and arrests. The FIA director general noted that regional cooperation was growing as countries combined resources to tackle shared threats. “We are also building capacity at home. NCBs develop training programmes for national police to raise awareness of Interpol’s tools and databases so that our officers can use them effectively on the ground,” Anwar said. “FIA NCB-Interpol Pakistan remains committed to ensuring that no fugitive finds safe haven abroad. Through I-24/7 and our network of partners, we will keep pursuing criminals and bringing them to justice.” In April this year, Interpol issued Red Notices against Bahria Town owner Malik Riaz and his son Ali Riaz, Nat­i­onal Accountability Bur­eau (NAB) Chairman Lt General (retired) Nazir Ahmed said. Last month, the National Cybercrime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) arrested two suspects and initiated the process for obtaining Red Notices for the remaining four alleged members of the “Tycoon2FA Cybercrime Network”.

Pakistan through to Women’s Asia Cup semi-finals as Nashra leads Hong Kong rout. Pakistan booked their place in the Women’s Asia Cup semi-finals after spinner Nashra Sandhu’s triggered a 72-run drubbing of Hong Kong, China at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium on Monday night. Nashra took six wickets as Pakistan defended 143 runs — that included a stand-out contribution by Shawaal Zulfiqaar — to set their last-four date against Sri Lanka on Friday. Pakistan skipper Fatima Sana, for the third match in a row, chose to bat first, looking to undo the damage of Pakistan’s hefty seven-wicket loss against India at the same venue on Saturday, where they were bowled out for their lowest ever T20 international score. The teams were unchanged from their previous matches, both of which came against India. Pakistan once again got off to a steady start with the bat, with openers Muneeba Ali and Shawaal easing their way to a 24-run opening partnership in three overs until Muneeba, who was too early on a shot, was bowled by Iqra Sahar. Gull Feroza at number three continued her unconvincing run in the tournament as she was dismissed leg-before-wicket on three off four balls after two consecutive ducks in the previous matches. Ayesha Zafar got off to a swift start with back-to-back boundaries when she came out to bat at number four to join Shawaal at the crease. Shawaal played perhaps the most convincing knock coming from a Pakistan batter this tournament, constructing a discerning yet well-paced knock of 47 off 35 balls, rotating strike and sending the odd ball away to ensure Pakistan could launch off a stable base. Ayesha Zafar fell after a handy knock of 26 off 19 balls, mistiming Joyleen’s Kaur slower tossed-up delivery, and unable to get it through the in-field. The wicket meant Pakistan were 82-3 at the halfway mark of their batting innings. Pakistan once again suffered from a middle-overs wobble as Shawaal, Sadaf Shamas and Eyman Fatima lost their wickets — all of them to Kaur — within the space of nine runs, with the team suddenly finding themselves at a shaky 101-6. Fatima (run-a-ball 24 not out) calmed Pakistan’s jitters, taking the team to 127 along with Tuba Hassan (14 off 13), who hit a four and a six off Kary Chan’s bowling before muddling an attempt to come down the track and getting bowled by her. Though the last two overs were quiet, coupled with the wicket of Umm-e-Hani, a six off the penultimate ball by the captain meant Pakistan ended their innings at 143-8, an above par total on a tricky pitch. Disciplined start Pakistan got off to a splendid start with the ball, with Fatima and Sadia Iqbal striking in consecutive overs, leaving Hong Kong at 1-2 at the two-over mark. Fatima bowled Mariko Hill off the last ball of the first over, ending a run-less Asia Cup campaign for the batter, while Sadia pinned Miles lbw off her first ball. Yasmin Daswani and Kary Chan fought well, putting together a 31-run partnership off 44 balls and ensuring Pakistan’s moments of indiscipline with the ball were punished. Nashra’s spectacular evening The introduction of Nashra, however, was not just decisive for Pakistan, but all-crushing for Hong Kong. She caught and bowled Daswani for the third wicket, breaking Hong Kong’s resistance and then single-handedly opened the floodgates. She dismissed Marina Lamplough soon after, before tempting Bibi to play across the line — which she did, ultimately getting caught by Sadaf at midwicket. Shanzeen Shahzad did the same, caught by Sadia at extra-cover, and Alison Siu was bowled on the very next ball, with Nashra securing her maiden T20I five-wicket haul. She soon became the first Pakistani to get a six-wicket haul in T20 internationals, as she bowled Sahar off the last ball of her four-over spell, finishing on stellar figures of 6-7. With Nashra having ripped through the line-up, Hong Kong eventually were bowled out for 71 runs, their innings extended only because of missed chances in the field by Pakistan. Umm-e-Hani took the final wicket of Joyleen Kaur to secure the 72-run win for Pakistan. Nashra was unsurprisingly named player of the match. With this result, Hong Kong, who needed to chase the total in 12.3 overs to qualify for the semi-finals were knocked out, while Pakistan secured a spot in the final four.

JI submits six proposals as first round of talks with govt concludes. ISLAMABAD: The first round of talks between Jamaat-i-Islami and the federal government on abolishing the petroleum levy and providing relief to the public concluded in Islamabad on Monday, with the party submitting six key proposals to the government committee. Both sides agreed to hold the next round on Thursday. Last week, the government and JI agreed to form committees comprising experts to discuss recommendations for reducing the petroleum levy and providing relief to the public. The JI delegation was led by Vice Emir Liaqat Baloch and comprised Deputy Secretary Syed Farasat Shah, KP Emir Inayatullah Khan, Lahore Emir Advocate Ziaur Rehman Ansari, Islamabad Emir Nasrullah Randhawa, Naveed Ali Baig and Shahid Naeem. Meanwhile, the government side was headed by Federal Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal and included Prime Minister’s Adviser Rana Sanaullah, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and State Minister for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani. Addressing the media after the meeting on Monday, Baloch said they had presented six detailed proposals to the prime minister’s team, emphasising that the “direct Rs80 petroleum levy per litre on petrol and diesel is severely impacting the national economy”. He clarified that peaceful sit-ins and protests across the country would continue while negotiations proceeded. “The primary objective remains providing immediate relief to the public,” Baloch added, urging rulers to cut state expenditures as sufficient budgetary margin exists to accommodate tax relief. Baloch also expressed concern over unfulfilled government commitments made during previous talks regarding independent power producers (IPPs), adding that daily petroleum pricing should be discontinued. He also noted that the current subsidy structures had failed to deliver and provide relief to the public. Baloch said it was encouraging that the government had always given priority to negotiations. He reiterated that dialogue was the only solution and said JI also understood that protests were not a solution. However, he told the government that public frustration was increasing due to rising electricity, gas and petrol prices. The party leader further said, “We know that we are caught in the IMF’s grip and that many decisions are being taken by the government out of compulsion.” Addressing the media, Iqbal said that the government had invited JI for talks to seek its actionable suggestions, which had now been formally received. The minister added that the meeting had been convened to review JI’s proposals regarding the petroleum levy in detail, adding that there were certain national economic realities that could not be denied. He noted that the relevant government institutions would review the recommendations and that any impractical points would be discussed openly with JI during the upcoming session. The planning minister said the government never wanted to overburden citizens, but global economies had been disrupted by regional tensions, including the US-Israeli war on Iran. “Petroleum prices would naturally ease once regional conflicts de-escalate,” he added. He stressed that the government and all stakeholders were concerned about the public interest and that the government did not want to impose any additional burden on the people. “If any relief can be provided to the people in any way, we will be very happy ourselves,” he said. Responding to a question about the policy rate, he said the government did not determine it, as the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) was autonomous in this regard. He added that the SBP’s policy board decided the policy rate after taking inflation into account. Iqbal also announced the next course of action, saying JI’s proposals concerned various ministries and that the views of the relevant institutions would be sought on them. He said a second round of talks would be held within three days after feedback was received from the relevant institutions.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs358.77 per litre while HSD will cost Rs381.77 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable on Sept 8 (Tuesday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Legal challenge launched against PTI’s planned march on Islamabad. • IHC CJ Dogar to take up petition against Sept 27 protest today • Petitioner fears disruption of routine life, traffic, and businesses, seeks court intervention against use of provincial resources for march • KP CM asks Karachi lawyers to join protest, says Imran not cutting any deals ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has been moved against the PTI’s planned sit-in and nationwide protest scheduled for Sept 27, with the petitioner apprehending disruption of routine life, traffic and business activities in the federal capital. IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar will hear the petition filed by citizen Waqas Ahmed on Tuesday. The petitioner has made the inspectors general of police of all four provinces, Islamabad Police and Motorway Police, besides other relevant government authorities, as respondents. According to the petition, the PTI has announced a sit-in in Islamabad on Sept 27, which could cause inconvenience to citizens and commuters and adversely affect business activities in the capital. The petitioner particularly raised concerns over the proposed participation of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, who, according to the PTI’s announcement, would lead the Islamabad-bound protest. The petition expressed apprehension that the resources and machinery of the provincial government could be utilised for political activity. It sought directions to the provincial authorities not to involve themselves in any political activity and to confine themselves to their official responsibilities. The petitioner also sought appropriate directions to the respondents to ensure that the rights of ordinary citizens, commuters and business communities were not affected by the proposed protest. The petition came ahead of the PTI’s preparations for its Sept 27 mobilisation, which the party leadership declared would not remain confined to Islamabad. CM invites lawyers KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi spent the past few days in Sindh to mobilise the party supporters for the Sept 27 protest. Speaking at a convention organised by the Sindh High Court Bar Association on Monday, the CM, who reached Karachi despite hurdles, invited lawyers to participate in the PTI protest and maintained that his leader Imran Khan was standing firm for the future of the country and was not striking any deal for his release. He said the Islamabad High Court had ordered his meeting with the party founder, while the Supreme Court had ordered hospitalisation of former premier, but that was to no avail. He added the judiciary was reluctant to timely fix the contempt applications for hearings. The CM also complained about the obstacles on the route of his convoy. PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari posted a welcome message on social media while his party’s government in Sindh placed obstacles in the way of his convoy and arrested the participants. The CM apologised to the people of Sindh and Karachi for the inconvenience caused by his convoy’s movement. He, however, said the province already lacked adequate infrastructure and that even the available thoroughfares had been blocked. Sept 27 protest According to PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja, the party’s call for Sept 27 is aimed at mobilising people across the country for the supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, and release of PTI founder Imran Khan. He had clarified that demonstrations would be held in every city and district, maintaining that peaceful protest was a constitutional and legal right. “The people from every province and district would take to the streets as a nationwide, peaceful movement for their rights and the supremacy of the Constitution and law,” he had said. Mr Raja had further said that the Sept 27 protest would be “Pakistan’s voice” and that the party would exercise what it considered its constitutional and legal right to hold peaceful demonstrations. He had also confirmed that KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi would lead the Sept 27 long march towards Islamabad, desc­ribing the planned mobilisation as a nationwide movement. The preparations for the mobilisation have also seen the emergence of a volunteer organisation among PTI workers in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Last week, a group of ideological PTI workers announced the formation of a volunteer unit called ‘Pasdaran-i-Azm Imran Khan Pakistan’ to assist participants and provide support during the Sept 27 long march. Redrawing the map. IT has been quite something to watch a whisper become, in a matter of weeks, the state’s new “number one priority”. The trigger was the interior minister’s surprising admission at the Pakistan Economic Summit in late July that the present system had “collapsed”, and that new provinces and administrative reform were therefore urgently needed. The political earthquake was immediate. For the PPP, already fuming over the AJK election , it was an insult added to injury. The president’s abrupt departure for London has since fed a good deal of speculation. Some believe that he went to press his allies in government to drop the idea altogether. Others have pointed out that his exit echoes another, years ago, when the PPP was being asked to make choices it considered political suicide. What can be said with certainty, however, is that an impasse has been reached. The president had met the interior minister in London. Their interaction was recorded and shown in the media. It does not seem to have gone fruitfully. On his return, the minister doubled down on the need for new administrative units. The PPP answered with a Sindh Assembly resolution rejecting new provinces , and with speeches declaring “no compromise” on the province’s geographical unity. The Sindh Assembly resolution deserves much more attention than it received given the implications for the drive for more provinces. Under Article 239(4) of the Constitution, the limits of a province cannot be altered unless the amendment is first passed by that province’s own assembly by a two-thirds majority. Sindh seems to have made its position plain by, at least symbolically, vetoing the proposal before it arrived at its door. Before the country is dragged through another ugly crisis, those pushing for new provinces must explain how they intend to clear the bar set by the Constitution. They should also share what the new assemblies, secretariats and offices will cost, and where the money is to come from when citizens’ own pockets are already empty. There is no question that Pakistan needs better administrative management, but the stated end of restructuring — ie, better service delivery at the grassroots — is already provided for in Article 140A, and could be achieved far more cheaply by reviving, resourcing and actually holding elections for local governments. Here, the political parties also share blame. They have spent decades hollowing out the LG system and alienating the citizenry. Any party that is unwilling to empower even a district council should not be arguing that the province is the only unit that matters. Therefore, though the LG system remains a less politically toxic option, it will only be considered an option if the political parties themselves make a renewed commitment to it. This is something they, too, must understand. Published in Dawn, September 8th, 2026

Nepra clears key hurdle to competitive power market. • Approves uniform charges for all Discos; participating bulk power consumers to pay Rs6.23-Rs19.62 per unit • Clears path for first 400MW open-access electricity auction ISLAMABAD: The Nat­ional Electric Power Regu­latory Authority (Nepra) on Monday approved use of system charges (UoSC) ranging from Rs6.23 to Rs19.62 per unit for bulk power consumers (BPCs) of all distribution companies participating in the competitive electricity trading market. The approval paves the way for open-access consumers to participate in an upcoming 400-megawatt auction. The consumers will pay the fee to the national grid to transport electricity from the source to the user. The charge includes transmission and distribution costs, fixed grid charges and cross-subsidies. Put together, a B-3 industrial consumer will be charged Rs6.23 per unit by the national grid, while a B-4 industrial consumer will pay Rs9.09 per unit. These charges will be in addition to the power supply rate, including generation costs, to be settled between private-sector power suppliers and BPCs. Currently, there are more than 3,000 BPCs across the country. The UoSC for C-3 and C-2 single-point distribution consumers is set bet­ween Rs14.95 and Rs19.62 per unit. General supply consumers in the A-2 and A-3 categories will be charged Rs19.14 per unit. Bulk power consumers who choose not to participate in the competitive wheeling auction will face significantly higher transport rates, ranging from Rs19.17 to Rs32.56 depending on their category. Non-participating B-3 and B-4 consumers will be charged Rs19.17 and Rs25.45 per unit, respectively. C-2 and C-3 consumers will pay Rs31.30 and Rs32.56, while A-2 and A-3 categories face a Rs32.08 charge. A fixed grid charge of Rs1 per kilowatt per month, based on sanctioned load, will apply to all categories regardless of whether they participate in the competitive auction. The uniform rate announcement for all distribution companies, incl­uding K-Electric, is aimed at formally launching the competitive wholesale elec­t­ricity market. Under the first phase, the Inde­pendent System Oper­ation (ISMO), a new power division entity, will auction 400MW of electricity within the next few months. The government has already allocated 800MW for auction in two phases. Nepra issued the determination after reviewing submissions from the Power Division, ISMO, K-Electric and BPCs regarding the mechanism for determining and settling UoSC, including inter-Disco differentials, cross-subsidies and transmission and distribution (T&D) losses. The Power Division had proposed that the impact of inter-DISCO differentials arising from uniform application of UoSC should not be imposed solely on wheeling consumers. Nepra had earlier circulated a draft adjustment mechanism among relevant stakeholders for settling inter-Disco differentials. The regulator said the key principle was to ensure that UoSC applicable to open-access consumers remained equal to those applicable to similarly placed consumers of suppliers of last resort (SOLRs). Based on the T&D losses of individual Discos, Nepra determined a uniform loss factor of 8.04 per cent at the 11kV level. For consumers connected at 132kV, the regulator approved a uniform loss factor of 1.51pc, as suggested by the Power Division. Nepra ruled that the additional charge would apply to all consumers, inc­luding open-access consumers and SOLR consumers, to cover differences among distribution companies and K-Electric while maintaining uniformity. The federal government had already appr­oved framework guidelines for the wheeling auction of 800MW of electricity through bilateral competitive trading and to move towards integrated energy planning across Pakistan. Under the guidelines, 800MW of generation capacity will be sold through a competitive auction for five years. The volume will gradually increase after the initial trial phase, subject to government approval. Nepra was tasked with determining uniform wheeling and grid charges for bulk power consumers. ISMO will now formally conduct an auction for 400MW under a process approved by Nepra a few days ago. The entity will announce the auction calendar and detailed procedures within days, without imposing an upper or lower limit on bid values, which will remain fixed for one year. Under timelines set under the IMF programme, approval of the auction guidelines was targeted for December, while Nepra’s approval of uniform wheeling charges was scheduled for January 2026. Both deadlines have already been met. Published in Dawn, September 8th, 2026

Seven GB roads set for federal takeover to boost tourism. • 464km of thoroughfares to be rehabilitated, maintained by NHA • Federal cabinet to consider proposal after approval by GB cabinet • Roads frequently damaged by landslides and flash floods • Tour operators, hotel owners and transporters welcome PM’s initiatives GILGIT: The federal government has identified seven roads spanning 464 kilometres across Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) for federalisation under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s tourism initiative, with the routes to be constructed, widened, rehabilitated and maintained by the federal authorities to improve connectivity and promote tourism in the mountainous region. An official of the National Highway Authority (NHA) told Dawn that Federal Communications Minister Abdul Aleem Khan had proposed to the GB government that seven key roads across the region be handed over to the Centre under PM’s tourism initiative. The seven roads identified include the 54km Astore-Chilim Chowki Road, 31km Deosai-Skardu Road, 100km Skardu-Khaplu Road, 17km Skardu (Thorgu)-Shigar Road and the 36km Karakoram Highway-Naltar to Satrangi Lake Road. The remaining two routes, the 121km Thalichi-Astore-Rattu-Shounter Road and the 105km Gorikot-Shagarthang-Skardu Road, are currently under construction. The NHA official said the proposal had been approved by the GB cabinet and a memorandum of understanding (MoU) had also been signed in this regard. The move comes as the government seeks to expand tourism infrastructure in the region, where difficult terrain and limited road connectivity remain major challenges to exploiting its tourism potential. The initiative is aimed at strengthening road connectivity to some of the region’s major tourism destinations, improving access to remote communities and facilitating travel across GB. Roads in GB are frequently blocked by landslides, mudflows, heavy rainfall, avalanches, flash floods and glacial lake outburst floods (Glofs). NHA’s role Under the plan, the roads will be constructed, widened, rehabilitated and maintained by the NHA to improve connectivity and facilitate access to popular tourist destinations. The official said that the proposal would be placed before the federal cabinet for approval. Once approved, the NHA would assume responsibility for the development and long-term upkeep of the seven road links, including their construction, widening, rehabilitation and maintenance. Asked about funding, he said the federal government would provide funds for the project. Previously, the GB government had been bearing the cost of maintenance, widening and rehabilitation of the roads, he added. The official said it had also been proposed that a toll tax be introduced for tourists visiting the scenic region, with a blanket exemption for local residents. Revenue generated through the toll would be spent on improving the road network in GB, he said. “With the number of tourists to Gilgit-Baltistan multiplying each year, the federal minister proposed introducing a toll tax to fund road infrastructure development. However, locals should be exempt from this tax,” the official said. Move appreciated People associated with the tourism sector, including hotel owners and transporters, welcomed the initiative and expressed hope that improved road maintenance and connectivity would help promote tourism. Ikram Baig, president of the GB Association of Tour Operators, told Dawn that the initiative would help promote tourism in the region. He said frequent road blockages were a serious issue for GB, as tourists were not only stranded for several days but residents also faced similar difficulties during bad weather. He said there was hope for an improved road network in the region after the federal government assumed responsibility for the roads. “This initiative can boost tourism. Delays in restoring road connectivity and frequent blockages have badly affected tourism in GB,” he said, adding that a reliable road network was essential for the sector. Ayaz Ahmed Shigri, general secretary of the Alpine Club of Pakistan and owner of a guest house, said poor road connectivity remained a major hurdle to promoting tourism. He too believed that the initiative would help enhance tourism in GB. Asghar Khan, manager of Serena Hotel, told Dawn that tourists usually planned their visits according to fixed schedules. He said frequent road blockages disrupted tourists’ plans and sometimes left them stranded in the region for days. Such situations created a negative impression and discouraged tourists from visiting the region, he said. “Many tourists, including national and international visitors, cancelled their plans to visit because of blocked roads,” Mr Khan said. He said the federal government’s decision to take responsibility for the roads could help reduce the problem if the plan was implemented in its true spirit. GB Tourism Minister Naiknaam Karim said accessibility played a major role in tourism development. He said if the federal government took responsibility for the roads, the NHA could ensure better management and improvement of the network with greater resources. Clichés we use. CONVERSATIONS about Pakistan easily and comfortably slide into clichés. The phrase ‘land of the pure’ is a personal favourite. Different generations — from boomers all the way down to the millennials — are perhaps equally familiar with ‘Pakistan at a crossroads’. Used as a headline or caption, it can be comfortably deployed to describe the state of affairs within, regardless of the context — be it the time of the Cold War, or the post 9/11 world, or from democratic interludes to hybrid times. The guilt is not just of Pakistanis but also the rest of the world which sees the country through a fog of clichés. Within this hard country, or the most dangerous country in the world, are the leafy streets of Islamabad, the port city of Karachi and Lahore with its Mughal past. Politics is military-dominated, and people have a penchant for strongmen in uniform, while political parties are family enterprises. KP is known as the province of the warrior-like Pathans, and Balochistan is tribal. Sindh is feudal territory where generations of peasants have worshipped Sufis and the Bhuttos. While the descriptions may vary a bit, they all portray societies frozen in time where little has changed, politically and socially. Agreed that many of these clichés are the result of foreign coverage of a country that has been, for various reasons, open to the storytelling by others. But at this point, it is hard to say if the storytelling by others has shaped our thinking and analysis or vice-versa. Whatever the case, clichés now shape so much of opinion that even society at large has been oblivious to the changes taking place under their very noses. For instance, it took 20 years of an insurgency in Balochistan for most people to realise that the sardars were no longer in charge in the province; the cliché has yet to be abandoned in discussions and by those who want to control politics. Indeed, clichés are used not just to describe but also to define how the country’s politics is run. The latter continues to be dominated by dynasties; people are uneducated and don’t know how to vote for the right people — which is why democracy doesn’t work. For they don’t vote for ‘good’ people but for those who can help them with gali, mohallay ki siyasat , or local issues. Or they voted for personalities and cult leaders. The cliché might alter a bit here and there but the inability of the people to make the right choice doesn’t. It’s enough to try the patience of a saint. Or many among our stability-seeking saints. But the politicians have their own set of clichés, convinced that only their capability can save the country — be it the ability to make a deal, a road (or rather, many roads), or end corruption. No one else is good enough. To their credit, none of them think they can aspire to learn the art a rival may have mastered. With their one skill, they can save Pakistan, much like the heroes of yesteryear who wore shorts over skinny pants and worked alone to save the Metropolis or Gotham. But this is an old cliché — before Hollywood discovered that they could all be made to fly together to confront the bad guys. Others, too, view them through clichés — cults, populists, experienced politicians, deal makers. And then the favourite is about how all of them were born in the same nursery (of the green and brown kind). Or as the latest version in Urdu goes, they passed through the same gate, the point being that none of them is authentic or genuine enough. Till, of course, they suffer at the same hands. The cycle repeats itself each time — with a new Pygmalion; a new flower seller. And then come the clichés about how to fix this country. These, too, have not changed. In one of the clichés, the problem is always the older, more established politician. And their removal is the answer. Minus one at times, minus everyone at others. It was Bhutto back in the 1970s and Nawaz Sharif in the 1990s. And these days, it seems it’s Imran Khan . Another is to rid the country of ‘kruption’; so what if each such effort seems to have done little to stop the scourge, which is growing by leaps and bounds. It’s a cliché, not reality. But there is an even better one. The effort to ensure a better, truer democracy. And it is never the politicians who are interested in this cliché; others always have it on hand to help the people, and give them better leaders and a rosier future. Its name keeps changing but not the good intentions. Sometimes, it means partyless elections, sometimes empowered local governments, one unit or more provinces . Call a rose by any other name and all that. It is so familiar and yet so different. For the dream hasn’t changed even though the times have. So it appears the old system needs more than a reset. It needs an overhaul so powers are devolved and people are helped at their doorstep. And this time around, we don’t just need random educated, middle class people in power, but those who can be compared to say Sadiq Khan in London or Zohran Mamdani in New York. There was a time when Mustafa Kamal was what the people of Karachi (and beyond) deserved as nazim but now the aspiration is not as local as it was then. Times have changed — or have they, in the land of the pure, also known as Cliché-stan? The writer is a journalist. Published in Dawn, September 8th, 2026

SC upholds Bait-ul-Mal aid for Hindu girls. • Rejects plea against SHC order requiring Pakistan Bait-ul-Mal to pay Rs10,000 per month to each girl, with 10pc annual increase until marriage • CJP says courts may look beyond legal questions to address underlying predicament ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a plea filed by the Pakistan Bait-ul-Mal (PBM) challenging the Sindh High Court’s Dec 1, 2022, order directing the welfare institution to provide financial support to two Hindu minor girls. A three-judge SC bench, headed by Chief Justice of Pakistan (CJP) Yahya Afridi and comprising Justice Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Justice Miangul Hassan Auran­gzeb, upheld the SHC Larkana Circuit Court’s order requiring the PBM to register the minors as beneficiaries for payment of monthly maintenance of Rs10,000 each, with an annual increase of 10 per cent, until their marriage. Though the Supreme Court appreciated the concern shown by the high court for the welfare of the minors, it laid down a framework for future cases, stating that cases should be referred to the PBM for consideration where circumstances disclosed before a court appear to warrant recourse to the institution. Bait-ul-Mal may thereafter facilitate the applicant by assessing their circumstances in accordance with the applicable policy and eligibility criteria and determining the extent of assistance. “This course allows the concerned court to bring a deserving case within the reach of the welfare institution established to respond to it, without displacing the structure through which the PBM is required to administer its assistance,” the court observed. The controversy stemmed from PBM’s challenge to the Dec 1, 2022, SHC order, which held that Ram Raj — the paternal grandfather of the two minor Hindu children — was not personally liable for their maintenance under the applicable family law. However, the high court also directed Bait-ul-Mal to register the minors as regular beneficiaries and pay each of them monthly maintenance. It so happened that Shrimati Re­eta, a Hindu woman, married Ravi Kumar in 2012, and two minor daughters, Jasika and Sanika, were born of the marriage. Ravi Kumar later died by suicide on May 20, 2017. With no independent source of income to maintain herself and her daughters after her husband’s death, Shrimati Reeta instituted proceedings before a family court in Jacobabad, seeking maintenance for the minors from one of the respondents, their paternal grandfather, Ram Raj. Ram Raj’s own circumstances were scarcely better. Aged and infirm, he too lacked a source of income and a residence of his own and was living in a dharamshala (charitable shelter). Nevertheless, the family court decreed the claim for maintenance and directed Ram Raj to pay Rs3,000 per month to each minor, with an annual increase of 10pc. The decree was maintained in appeal, after which Ram Raj invoked the constitutional jurisdiction of the SHC. CJP Afridi observed in the judgement that courts were not infrequently faced with cases where resolution of the legal question at hand did not necessarily resolve the underlying predicament of the parties. Thus, in fully discharging its judicial function, a court may look beyond the immediate legal question and seek to address that predicament. And when a state institution exists precisely for that purpose, the court may very well seek its assistance, he observed. The present case, the CJP noted, demonstrated precisely why such recourse may sometimes become necessary. The judgement noted that the minors’ mother was a widow without an independent source of income, while their paternal grandfather, himself aged and infirm, was living in destitute conditions. The judgement noted that the two children belonged to a religious minority in a country where minorities occupied a particularly vulnerable position, with social and economic hardships often bearing upon them with greater force. While poverty, loss of familial support and other forms of hardship were difficult to withstand in themselves, their impact might be considerably more acute for those who already stood outside the social majority, the verdict said. Therefore, institutions of the state must remain mindful of this reality, the judgement said, adding that for Jasika and Sanika, their minority status formed a crucial part of the wider context in which their need for support should be considered.
