The perpetual weak link. IS India a weak link that worries the architects of the Shanghai club and the BRICS group? The question is as urgent today as it ever was, its importance underscored further by a potentially crucial BRICS summit that Prime Minister Narendra Modi hosts later this month. Several factors may be at play to determine if India is indeed a weak link for BRICS. Every country has its core interests and India’s foreign policy today seems to be based on two key factors, one being the calculation as to who or what can best help deliver the core interest of the ruling elite, namely the consolidation of a majoritarian state, the Hindu rashtra. It’s all too well known that the financial foundations of Hindutva lie in the West, a fact that became even more obvious with the recent visit by the head of the RSS to the US and Canada . Russia and China have scant interest in the ruling party’s ideology as long as it does not disturb the political furniture the two groups have worked hard to set up. The West, too, couldn’t care less about the dominant worldview of a country as long as it is a trusted ally. A classic indication here is the silent acceptance of Israel’s genocide of Palestinians . When Western human rights groups mount pressure on India over its treatment of religious and ethnic minorities, it’s more of a leverage to extract political outcomes than a pursuit of moral tenets. A second factor in framing foreign policy is the interest of major business houses aligned with the Modi government. A typical episode showed India’s vulnerability in the Adani affair in the US. The political quid pro quo to get relief in the corruption case would be hard to assess, but it would be equally hard to ignore. In the middle of this equation, a nagging frustration stalks Narendra Modi’s battle to project himself to the world as a visionary from India, most recently in the image of Mahatma Gandhi and Gautam Buddha. Last week, Modi cast himself in the role of the two visionaries he cited to Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, telling the Russian leader to terminate the war in Ukraine so that the world could live in peace and prosperity. Putin is always inclined to be patient with India given the importance he attaches to New Delhi’s membership of the Shanghai club and the BRICS orbit amid the groups’ sharpening battle with the US dollar and Donald Trump’s revulsion at a multipolar world, which much of Asia, Africa and Latin America seeks. A nagging frustration stalks Narendra Modi’s battle to project himself to the world as a visionary from India. Putin heard out Modi, eyes lowered and feet tapping in lieu of rudely looking at his wristwatch. Donald Trump, too, wants Russia to terminate the war as does Europe, preferably by weakening Moscow and, if possible, by delivering a strategic defeat. They pine for the elusive outcome without leaning on any moral principles, though. To them, as for much of the world, wars are politics by other means. What is less discussed in the Indian media is the fact that the war between Russia and Ukraine was set off by the US and its European satellites, which had ignored Putin’s red lines and sought to plant Nato’s battle formations right on Russia’s borders. The war became imminent when the West staged a colour revolution to oust a Russia-friendly government in Kiev and installed one that would eventually lead to Volodymyr Zelensky’s elevation as the West’s costly catspaw. Modi’s message of peace in elliptical geometry — “move from unending war to end of war” — did not go unnoticed by those who witnessed India’s bruising conflict with Pakistan in May last year . Initiated as revenge for an unconscionable terror attack on Hindu tourists in Pahalgam , the war was curiously suspended with Trump’s self-proclaimed intervention but not closed. War or no war, hostility to Pakistan remains a major input in the consolidation of Hindutva. In other words, the tensions with nuclear-armed Pakistan and India could go kinetic at the time of nuclear-armed India’s choosing, Buddha’s and Gandhi’s moral tenets notwithstanding. Both revered legends were the eminences grises in the Nehruvian concept of the modern welfare state he wanted India to become. And Nehru’s idealism flowed equally from his belief in the Soviet system of a command economy as the one best suited to alleviate mass poverty created and deepened by the colonial plunder of India. Mao’s China, too, was moving along the path Nehru extolled, except that Nehru placed his quest in the framework of democracy. A similar path was followed by Deng Xiaoping’s economic liberalisation and Xi Jinping’s market consolidation, with neither leader loosening the grip on the command economy. “Horse racing will continue, stocks will continue to be traded, and dancing will continue,” Deng prophesied with the return of Hong Kong to China in 1997. Nehru’s fear of untethered capitalism sprang from his astute assessment that a system instinctively rooted in private profit was unworthy of trust for the impoverished masses. How true his instinct was can be glimpsed from the 800 million Indians on the food dole despite four decades of a World Bank- and IMF-prescribed free-market system. Modi’s desperation to be deemed a worthy heir to his iconic compatriots relies on his near-total control of the media. The frustration with failing to fit into the oversized shoes of Jawaharlal Nehru as statesman and prime minister, respected and admired widely at home and abroad, however, is particularly galling. The self-advertised image as a culturally inclusive leader banks on the goodwill earned by India’s freedom heroes, none of whom came from the Hindutva fold. Modi’s dual personality charge is occasionally reflected in his angry frown at home together with a free flow of invectives hurled at opponents and the ready laughter and embraces abroad. China and Russia would not be too worried by Modi’s dual personalities. What might perhaps concern them more is Hindutva’s deeply fraught investment in the West. Similarly, residents pay income tax, stamp duty, land transfer fees and many more taxes, while in return, they get nothing from the NFC Award,” he said. The local MNA further said that without provincial status, the issues of Islamabad’s residents could not be addressed properly. “In urban areas, the CDA, after selling its land, carries out development work. While for rural areas, we have to request the federal government for various packages and most of the time we remain unsuccessful. Therefore, an NFC share is the only solution,” he said. Mr Nawaz said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had formed a committee under the supervision of Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, which had already shared its recommendations with the premier, proposing the devolution of powers from the federation to the ICT as a federating unit. Under these proposals, “we want a provincial-style government for Islamabad,” he said. It is relevant to note that under the proposal, the Islamabad Assembly will have 27 members, 21 directly elected members, seven from each of the three NA constituencies, five women on reserved seats and one minority member. The proposed assembly will elect a leader, who will be called chief minister or mayor and will serve as the chief executive, while the chief commissioner will be replaced with a chief secretary. Mr Nawaz said that under the proposals, all departments would function under the assembly, except law and order and master planning, as these two functions would remain under the federal government. Asked whether, if the government went ahead with the plan to provide provincial status to Islamabad, the ECP would have to carry out fresh delimitation, he said, “No issue. We don’t want to hold ineffective local government elections like those held in 2015-16. We want an efficient and vibrant system to resolve public issues.” Amid the proposal, elections in Islamabad are likely to face further delay, as experts say that if the government goes ahead with the proposals, changes to the Local Government Act or its replacement with a new law, as well as amendments to the CDA Ordinance, would be required before fresh delimitation for the elections. Therefore, the already announced local government delimitation process is likely to face a setback. Currently, the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) is carrying out delimitation and, according to its schedule, the election body is supposed to publish details of the final constituencies and Union Councils on October 14, 2026. The next step would be the announcement of the election schedule. However, it now appears that the elections will face further delay. The term of the last local government in Islamabad expired in February 2021, and since then elections have been delayed under various pretexts. As a result, around 2.5 million residents of Islamabad continue to face issues ranging from water shortages to unpaved streets. On several occasions, the federal government decided to hold elections only to cancel them later under various pretexts, mainly to “further strengthen” the Local Government Act for “better performance”. Earlier, in January this year, President Asif Ali Zardari approved an ordinance that introduced several amendments to the Local Government Act 2015. Besides replacing the Metropolitan Corporation Islamabad (MCI) with three town corporations, the ordinance gave the government-appointed administrator more powers and an indefinite tenure. The new ordinance was introduced at a time when local government elections in Islamabad were scheduled to be held on February 15. Thousands of people from all 125 Union Councils had already submitted nomination papers for the elections. Meanwhile, the ordinance also stated that in the absence of a local government, the administrator could hold office until new local government elections were held, replacing the provision that the administrator’s tenure could not exceed six months. The ordinance also empowered the administrator to levy taxes, fees, rates, rents, toll charges or surcharges. It is relevant to note that when the election schedule was announced by the ECP in February 2026, the local chapter of the PTI had claimed that the government, fearing defeat, would opt for an escape route and not conduct the elections in February. However, former PML-N deputy mayor Syed Zeeshan Ali Naqvi rejected the PTI’s claim, stating that the ordinance had been introduced for a better local government system in Islamabad and adding that the PML-N would win the elections. When the local government’s term ended in 2021, the PTI was in power and elections were supposed to be held within 120 days. However, the PTI government did not take serious steps to conduct the polls. When the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM) came into power, it too delayed the elections, while the incumbent government has so far also failed to conduct them. Published in Dawn, September 8th, 2026

The IWT ruling and the coming age of water coercion. The Court of Arbitration’s latest ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty deserves attention far beyond Pakistan and India. On August 31, the Court unanimously reaffirmed that the Treaty remains fully in force and rejected the grounds advanced by India for placing it in “abeyance”. It also imposed interim restrictions on specified construction at the Ratle Hydroelectric Plant while the Treaty’s adjudicatory processes continue. The immediate legal consequence is straightforward: India remains bound by the obligations it accepted under the 1960 Treaty. The wider significance is, however, more consequential. As water stress intensifies and upstream infrastructure expands, geographical control over rivers will increasingly create strategic leverage. The Court’s decision therefore arrives at an important moment. It establishes that physical advantage does not confer unlimited political discretion, and that binding obligations cannot be switched off through unilateral declarations. There is another aspect of the decision with potentially wider consequences for international law. India explicitly linked the Treaty’s continued operation to its allegations of cross-border terrorism, declaring in April 2025 that the IWT would remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” ended such support. The Court examined terrorism alongside the other grounds invoked publicly by India, including sovereignty, alleged material breach, changing circumstances and armed conflict. It found that none provided a legal basis for suspending or terminating the Treaty. That finding matters well beyond the Indus basin. An unjust correlation International law would become dangerously unstable if treaty obligations could be made contingent upon unilateral accusations arising from another sphere of interstate relations. Terrorism is a grave security issue and states retain the rights available to them under international law to address it. A water-sharing treaty, however, cannot be suspended merely because one party attaches a security allegation to its bilateral relationship with another. Otherwise, contested political claims could become self-created escape clauses from international obligations. The chronology makes the attempted linkage particularly difficult to sustain. The disputes concerning India’s Kishenganga and Ratle hydroelectric designs long predate the April 2025 attack that India subsequently cited in placing the Treaty in abeyance. Pakistan initiated the present arbitration in August 2016. Ratle’s design had been under dispute years earlier, while Kishenganga had already been the subject of international adjudication well before the latest deterioration in relations. The Court itself drew attention to this chronology when considering India’s arguments. This distinction is important. International adjudication serves, among other purposes, to separate legal obligations from the fog of political accusation and propaganda that often accompanies interstate crises. Once allegations from an unrelated security dispute are allowed to determine whether a treaty continues to bind, legal predictability gives way to political discretion. The stronger party gains the ability to define both the grievance and the consequence. That danger will grow as water becomes more strategically valuable. The stress of water A report by the World Resources Institute forecasts that the demand for water worldwide may increase by 20-25 per cent by 2050, and another billion people will experience very high risk of water stress. Over three billion people have already become reliant on transboundary water systems. In many of these basins, geography produces an unavoidable asymmetry: one country controls infrastructure upstream while another depends upon predictable flows downstream. Modern hydrological leverage can also be exercised without dramatically “turning off” a river. Reservoir operations, the timing of releases, construction choices and control over hydrological information can influence agriculture, electricity generation, flood planning and economic confidence downstream. The Mekong illustrates this emerging reality. Research by the Stimson Centre’s Mekong Dam Monitor has documented how upstream dam operations can significantly alter downstream flows during periods of scarcity. The significance lies in the capability created by infrastructure. An upstream state can acquire considerable influence over the timing and predictability of water reaching countries hundreds or thousands of kilometres away. The Nile presents another expression of hydrological asymmetry. Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam has demonstrated how a major upstream project can alter political calculations across an entire basin, where development priorities, national sovereignty and downstream water security intersect. Why it all matters These cases suggest that 21st century water coercion may look different from the old predictions of “water wars”. It can operate in the grey zone: through infrastructure, uncertainty, technical decisions and political pressure that remain below the threshold of armed conflict. This is precisely why the durability of the Indus Waters Treaty matters. For more than six decades, it has placed one of the world’s most politically sensitive river systems within an agreed legal framework. It has endured wars, military crises and prolonged periods of diplomatic hostility because its obligations do not depend upon the political temperature of the day. The latest ruling reinforces that principle. The Indian argument on sovereignty poses the exact same problem. Treaty making is in itself an exercise of sovereignty. The states become bound on a voluntary basis because it is mutual restraint rather than unilateral power that lends predictability and stability to the exercise of individual right. Sovereignty cannot subsequently become a mechanism for selectively suspending those obligations. If that principle were accepted, international agreements would become least reliable precisely during the crises for which durable agreements are most valuable. The Court’s interim measures concerning Ratle carry the same logic into the physical world. By restricting specified construction pending further determination, the Court has sought to prevent irreversible developments from prejudicing an ongoing legal process. In river disputes, concrete can create facts faster than adjudication can resolve them. The ability of a legal mechanism to preserve the status quo therefore has practical strategic significance. The Indus decision consequently offers a larger lesson for an increasingly water-stressed international system. Geography will continue to create asymmetries. Technology will increase the ability of upstream states to control infrastructure. Political crises will continue to generate allegations, retaliation and pressure. The safeguard lies in preventing those realities from overriding binding legal commitments. The Court has drawn that boundary clearly in the Indus case. Security accusations cannot unilaterally determine the life of a water treaty. Sovereignty cannot erase obligations voluntarily undertaken. And upstream geography cannot, by itself, become a licence for hydrological coercion. As competition over shared rivers grows, those principles may prove far more important than the dispute that brought them before the Court.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect as US trade talks stall. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect just after midnight on Tuesday as Prime Minister Mark Carney increased economic pressure on his country’s biggest trading partner after negotiations collapsed last month, intensifying an 18-month-old trade war. The counter-tariffs cover $20 billion of US goods, with duties ranging from 15 per cent to 50pc across products from steel and furniture to clothing and electronics. The dollar-for-dollar retaliation marks an escalation in the dispute between the neighbouring countries, and US and Canadian officials have traded blame for scuttling a deal that seemed close to fruition two weeks ago. The rising tensions create uncertainty about the broader US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement , which is up for annual reviews after US President Donald Trump declined to extend it for another decade. “What we are worried about is an escalatory spiral,” said Michael Harvey, executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance and a member of Carney’s advisory committee on bilateral US economic relations. “But at the same time, we totally understand that the prime minister needs to find areas of leverage,” Harvey said. US tariffs hit Canadian wine, furniture, dairy Trump’s tariffs implemented last month hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, covering $20 billion, or 5pc, of Canadian exports to the US. According to Canadian and US government data, Canada has shipped almost 68pc of total exports to the US this year, out of which roughly 80pc moved duty-free due to exemptions under the USMCA pact. Protections under the agreement have provided the domestic economy some resilience. The new tariffs, imposed under a Depression-era US law, do not allow Ottawa to exercise USMCA exemptions. Concerns about the USMCA’s future have fuelled uncertainty about investment and growth, as Canada wages a trade war against an economy 13 times its size. Polls show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but it could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts. Just 20pc of Americans approved of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Carney said last week his government was ready to sign a trade deal that benefits both countries. Trump threatened last month to raise US tariffs on all cars, trucks and automotive parts from Canada to 50pc starting January 1, and signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America. A government source said there are currently no talks between the two sides among ministers or government officials. “The Canadian government needs to keep channels open to the United States and not go overboard in terms of rhetoric and reacting to the rhetoric from the American side, while waiting for the American decision-making process to come back to economics,” Harvey said.

Why has oil stayed below $100 a barrel despite supply disruptions amid US-Iran escalation?. Global oil benchmark Brent crude has rallied this month but stayed below $100 a barrel despite recent escalation in the US-Iran conflict that has disrupted Gulf exports from the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Crude oil shipments from Middle East producers are at about 11 million barrels per day (bpd) now, from 18m bpd before the US-Israeli war on Iran began seven months ago, according to Argus. Here are some of the factors driving oil prices: Significant volumes have been able to flow through Hormuz In the week before fighting erupted again on August 30, roughly 8m to 9m bpd had been flowing through Hormuz, double the previous week’s volume, said Rystad Energy’s Chief Economist Claudio Galimberti. While flows have since fallen to below 2m bpd, the daily moving average is still around 4m to 5m barrels, which puts Brent at a “fair” price of $95, Galimberti said. Industry estimates put daily exports between 6m and 8m barrels. There has been no visible very large crude carrier exiting the strait since September 2, Kpler data showed on Monday. During the interim US-Iran peace deal in July, Hormuz exports touched pre-war levels of 16m bpd. Gulf exporters are using alternative routes and means Gulf producers have found alternative routes and are expected to continue sending cargoes for ship-to-ship transfers outside of Hormuz, mitigating some of the earlier shortfall. Saudi Aramco resumed loadings from its Ras Tanura port inside the Gulf in August, although its exports from Yanbu in the Red Sea remain under pressure from a naval blockade by the Yemeni Houthis. Yanbu exports hit a six-month low of 1.43m bpd in August, from an average of 3.9m bpd in the previous three months, provisional Kpler data showed. Exports from the alternative port of Egypt’s Sidi Kerir hit 2.14m bpd in August, more than double June volumes. Exports from No.2 Opec producer Iraq rebounded in August to around 2.34m bpd. Shipments from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) hovered around 2.9m bpd in August and July after hitting a record in June, Kpler data showed. Kuwaiti crude exports have recovered to about 1m bpd in July and August. However, Iran’s oil exports have fallen sharply due to the US blockade. Other producers are stepping up Non-Opec producers, including the US, Canada and Guyana, are set to increase output by a combined 1.4m bpd this year, according to Jarand Rystad, founder of Rystad Energy, partly filling the shortfall. Meanwhile, Russian crude exports held steady at about 5.5m bpd in July and August, down from the 6.4m bpd peak in June, but still 23 per cent higher than February as processing at Russian refineries has fallen due to damage to Russian plants from Ukrainian attacks, Kpler data showed. However, Russia has downgraded its 2026 oil output forecast to a 17-year low, which may reduce its exports. Demand destruction is significant Demand destruction in petrochemicals and transportation fuels remains significant in the third quarter at 3.5m bpd, versus 4.5m bpd in the second quarter, with China accounting for more than half of that due to rising transport electrification and coal-based chemicals, Rystad said. Top importer China, dubbed the “new demand Opec” for its market influence, slashed seaborne crude shipments to 7m bpd in July and August, from over 11m bpd in February. Beijing’s vast reserves, estimated by Kpler at 1.17 billion barrels, have also given markets comfort. Physical markets tell a different story Spot premiums have rebounded to April levels with Dubai and Oman at $19 to $20 a barrel above Dubai quotes for cargoes loading in November, Reuters data showed. Oman futures were at $104.54 a barrel on Monday while cash Dubai traded at $105.10 a barrel. “At the moment, it’s telling us that physically things are incredibly tight,” said David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus. “We’ve already got prices substantially above $100 a barrel and even more important, you’ve got a diesel market that is screaming shortage.” The recent US-Iran escalation is expected to curb Gulf exports while demand rises as refiners ramp output of diesel, which has hit a record high price in the US. Analysts lift forecast Several banks have raised their Brent price forecasts, including Morgan Stanley which expects prices averaging $100 a barrel in the fourth quarter. Goldman Sachs raised its Brent and West Texas Intermediate forecasts by $5 a barrel for December 2026 and 2027, citing an expectation that Middle East shipping disruptions will persist into next year. It now forecasts Brent at $85 a barrel and WTI at $80 for December 2026, and 2027 prices at $80 and $75 a barrel, respectively.

Paris opens probe into women staff being 'sidelined' during Eiffel Tower visit. Female employees at the Eiffel Tower were asked to step out of sight during a visit by a ​Hindu religious delegation at the weekend, according to union representatives, prompting a staff protest ‌and an investigation by Paris city authorities. A delegation of about 100 ​people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha, or BAPS, made ​a private visit to the Eiffel Tower on Saturday. The spiritual movement later apologised for “any pain or inconvenience caused” by the incident. The September 5 incident angered staff and drew criticism from French politicians, with the Hindu religious group later apologising. The Paris monument was set to reopen Tuesday after being closed late on Monday following a meeting between staff and management. The operating company that runs the Eiffel Tower, SETE, acknowledged that the Hindu delegation had requested the visit be organised so as to limit “interactions with women” and said that “these conditions should not have been accepted”. “To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower,” BAPS wrote in its statement on X. “Due to the size of our delegation, the visit was arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal operating hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others.” Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire ​said that an investigation would be launched “as soon as possible”. In a post on social media platform X, ‌he said ⁠he was aware of the employees’ anger and agreed their dissatisfaction was legitimate. “It is urgent that all light be shed on the facts that led to this protest,” Gregoire wrote. Eiffel Tower staff said in a statement that it condemned “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit by the delegation. “Instructions were given to female employees of the Eiffel Tower and to female employees of contractors to make themselves invisible in order to welcome this delegation,” the staff said in their statement, adding they were shocked to have been put in such a situation. “Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present,” the statement said. “As the delegation passed through, women were ⁠asked to leave their workstations so that men could take their places,” Diane Davoine, a ​union representative, told Reuters . Davoine said management apologised to staff over the incident. Yael Braun-Pivet, the president of ⁠the ​National Assembly, wrote in a post on X: “Welcoming others never ​means giving up our values. In France, women are fully present in public life. No one tells them to become ​invisible.”

Ferdinandh CABRERA / AFP Report 358 / Asia-Pacific 03 September 2026 20+ minutes Policing the Bangsamoro: Peace in the Southern Philippines Security continues to be a concern in the autonomous region of Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines. Law enforcement reforms and better coordination between the military and the police – as well as stronger gun control and better access to courts – could help stem the violence. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags Philippines What’s new? Despite a 2014 peace agreement, crime and violence continue to rack the Bangsamoro region in the southern Philippines. The military, which is still in charge of public safety, as well as the police and an array of local institutions are wrestling with outbreaks of fighting powered by easy access to firearms. Why does it matter? Local conflicts persist across the Bangsamoro, and the implementation of key provisions of the 2014 peace agreement remains well behind schedule. Entrenched clan feuds, political violence and criminal rackets make it hard to foster the trust in state institutions and social bonds needed to withstand future conflict. What should be done? Reforms to make regional law enforcement stronger, more professional and responsive to community needs are vital, as well as better coordination between the military and the police. Access to courts, control over firearms, and reinforced peacebuilding are also imperative to prevent the escalation of local violence and tackle its roots. Executive Summary The 2014 peace accord ended decades of conflict between the Philippine government and Moro Muslim separatists in what is now the Bangsamoro autonomous region. But violence still flares as clan feuds, political rivalries and criminal rackets rattle the region. The police struggle to keep pace, leaving the military as the dominant security force. Other institutions remain ill prepared for the challenge. Courts are slow and often fail to guarantee justice, while institutions tasked with maintaining peace in the region have been afflicted by political infighting between factions of the former insurgent movement, and have yet to become fully operational. A clearer division of responsibility between Manila and regional authorities, along with a broader recognition of the roots of local conflict and the recurrent outbreaks of violence they cause, will be crucial to improving security conditions. At the heart of these efforts should be a reform of the police, bolstering recruitment, internal discipline and community policing. Tighter gun control, targeted justice reforms and peacebuilding initiatives should complement these efforts. After decades of war between the Philippine government and Moro rebels, progress toward curbing violence in the Bangsamoro region since it became autonomous in 2019 has been patchy. While the largest armed movement in the region, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), has renounced armed struggle and shifted its attention to the regional parliament and government, flare-ups of competitive political violence now outweigh rebel or militant fighting with the state. Clan feuds and electoral rivalries drive vendettas that regularly displace entire communities and weaken state authority. Criminal rackets are rife and firearms are easy to get hold of, fuelling cycles of violence. Key aspects of the 2014 peace agreement, including its security provisions, remain unfulfilled. This includes rebel disarmament, but also the redeployment of the military to other parts of the country and the disarmament of private militias. One of the biggest challenges in the normalisation process, as the region’s transition from war to peace is officially called, remains policing. The issue of who should be in charge of maintaining peace and order was the subject of intense debate during peace talks and in crafting the region’s autonomy law. Granting the regional government authority to handle public security was one option, but in the end Manila retained policing power in the region. Even so, the national police has struggled to define its role in areas of the newly autonomous region that remain affected by violence. Meanwhile, the integration of Moro ex‑rebels into the police force has been painstakingly slow. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. The military has earned public respect after decades of fighting a counterinsurgency in the area, but it is ill suited to handling local conflicts over the long run. Manila is grappling with how best to manage these dilemmas by continuing to deploy the military while using the police as backup. This approach, however, runs counter to the national government’s broader strategy of pivoting away from counterinsurgency to focus instead on external defence. For communities across the Bangsamoro hit by recurrent waves of violence, help is not always ready to hand. Communities often see the police as weaker, more politicised (especially due to local powerbrokers’ influence) and less dependable than the military. The regional government has greater powers over local dispute resolution and is in charge of building the local justice system, but is struggling to use its resources and is roiled by infighting. Long distances, case backlogs and steep costs mean local courts are often inaccessible to the Bangsamoro’s poorest citizens. The judiciary’s shortcomings are exacerbated by frequent score-settling between rival clans or bands, which can turn the filing of a legal case in court after a killing into the pretext for a fresh round of blood-letting and retaliation from the perpetrator’s clan. A rich tradition of community-based conflict resolution across the region offers alternatives, but its interaction with formal institutions has been uneven, and disputes often end up resurfacing. Both the national and regional governments should undertake reforms to mitigate violence and build a firmer foundation for handling threats to security. Supporting and professionalising the police is critical, but building a credible force will depend on practical improvements rather than sweeping reforms. Sustained efforts to rethink force structure, training and anti-corruption initiatives would help create a service responsive to the region’s needs. The police should also work to build better relations with communities, above all by addressing their most urgent concerns. Recruiting and training community safety police officers could be one way of bridging that gap. Ensuring better coordination between the military and police is also imperative. One solution would be for the military to gradually step back, enabling the police to take on more responsibilities for the management of public order. The relative calm in parts of the region should make this shift possible in at least some areas. These innovations should be accompanied by institutional reforms. The Bangsamoro needs sturdier mechanisms for settling disputes. Judicial reforms are also essential. For now, the formal justice system in the Bangsamoro remains weak, slow and too hard for its citizens to access, undermining public confidence in the courts. Strengthening Bangsamoro courts of all kinds with resources and personnel is paramount. Lastly, there are simply too many guns in the region for its citizens to be safe. Deterring gun use and clamping down on the supply of illegal weapons are essential to halt firearms proliferation. Together, these reforms should help curb the drivers of local violence, steer the region away from cycles of conflict and ensure law enforcement is in the hands of professional institutions that are responsive to the people of the Bangsamoro. Much as it was a singular achievement to end decades of insurgency, communities will not feel safe until the peace gets the policing it needs. Introduction For over five decades, a secessionist war raged in the Philippines’ southernmost island of Mindanao. The Muslim Moro people – who long experienced discrimination in the country – agitated for self-determination. 1 The term “Moro” refers to Islamised people in the southern Philippines, comprising thirteen ethno-linguistic groups. Two main armed movements representing Moro Muslim communities emerged: the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and its post 1977 splinter, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). 2 For earlier reporting on the peace process and transition, see Crisis Group Asia Reports N°355, Peace in the Philippines: The Bangsamoro’s Moment of Truth ; N°331, Southern Philippines: Making Peace Stick in the Bangsamoro , 1 May 2023; N°323, Islamist Militancy in the Southern Philippines , 18 March 2022; N°322, Southern Philippines: Fostering an Inclusive Bangsamoro , 18 February 2022; N°313, Southern Philippines: Keeping Normalisation on Track in the Bangsamoro , 15 April 2021; and N°306, Southern Philippines: Tackling Clan Politics in the Bangsamoro , 14 April 2020. The Philippine government deployed its military, paramilitary auxiliaries, and police against these groups. Over 120,000 people died in a conflict that did huge harm to public trust in state institutions and propagated the spread of weapons across numerous communities. The 2014 peace accord between Manila and the MILF – which provided political and fiscal autonomy to the Moro people within the boundaries of the Philippine state – marked a vital step toward reconciliation. In 2018, the Philippine Congress passed the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which voters then endorsed in a two-stage plebiscite in early 2019, thereby creating the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The Bangsamoro Transition Authority, an interim government led by the MILF, assumed power that February. The interim authority exercises self-governance in the Bangsamoro region, home to more than four million people spread across five provinces. The peace agreement foresaw two parallel tracks to achieve full Bangsamoro autonomy. First, former rebels would run the interim regional administration, pass new laws and build institutions. This political track was meant to conclude with regional elections in 2022, but these have been postponed several times, and are now planned for September 2026. Secondly, a “normalisation” agenda was to guide the broader transition from war to peace; it includes issues such as rebel disarmament but also socio-economic development and policing in the region. 3 The normalisation process does not have a set deadline and instead relies on qualitative milestones; both sides are meant to sign an “Exit Agreement” after they have met their respective commitments. As with the political track, however, the normalisation process has fallen behind schedule. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Kinship networks, entrenched political clans, diverse ethnolinguistic identities, and the uneasy coexistence of emerging political parties with armed movements all shape the region’s public life. Talking about his movement’s transition from guerrilla warfare to governance, a senior MILF commander admitted: “It was easier in the jungle”. 4 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Political tensions have also flared within the former insurgency. In March 2025, Manila replaced the region’s chief minister, MILF Chairman Murad Ebrahim, with the organisation’s military chief, Abdulraof Macacua. This change fractured the movement, pitting commanders and cadres loyal to the Central Committee against Macacua’s faction. 5 Murad is closely aligned with MILF’s chief negotiator and head of its implementing panel Mohagher Iqbal, who wields substantial influence over the movement’s political cadres. In response to Macacua’s perceived violations of internal regulations, the Central Committee suspended both him and eight loyal senior commanders from their roles, stopping short of expelling them from the organisation. The Bangsamoro region governs itself – the interim government, for example, exercises control over public finances – but the state’s use of force remains under Manila’s control. Specifically, the national government retains command over the police, while the armed forces play an active role in ensuring security. This arrangement reflects the national government’s enduring caution about a region with a long history of rebellion and the Philippine constitution, which mandates just one police force. 6 Crisis Group interviews, Manila, 8 May 2026. See also Article XVI, Section 6 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution. Building on Crisis Group’s earlier work in the Bangsamoro, this report explores how public security is managed in the region, with particular attention to policing. It draws on years of field research in the Bangsamoro and Manila, including over 80 interviews with police and military officers, MILF commanders, representatives of the interim regional government, national and local officials, civil society figures, clan leaders, donors, villagers and decommissioned fighters. Women comprised around a third of interviewees. II. The Peace Deal and its Violent Aftermath Despite the undeniable progress made since the 2014 peace agreement, the Bangsamoro continues to grapple with security dilemmas. Although large-scale fighting has stopped, more than a third of young people across the region have experienced armed conflict within or near their homes since 2019. 7 Bangsamoro Youth Commission, “Bangsamoro Youth Assessment Study”, 2024, p. 60. A local civil society leader described the region as being in a state of “controlled peace”. 8 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Navigating sporadic outbursts of disorder remains particularly challenging for law enforcement. A. Conflict and Crime The national government now faces two main security threats in Mindanao. Its first concern are jihadist groups that have stayed out of the peace process and continue to fight the state. With the regional government’s support, Manila has managed to subdue cells from these outfits in the Sulu archipelago and contain groups in Central Mindanao. 9 Crisis Group interview, MILF commander, Cotabato City, 2 November 2023. The regional government has several programs to support fighters who gave up arms, and the MILF also played a role in influencing young Moros to cease armed struggle. But while their attacks on security forces have declined, these groups have not been decimated. 10 On 14 December 2025, a shooting at Sydney’s Bondi Beach claimed the lives of fifteen people at the hands of father and son, Sajid and Naveed Akram. In the weeks leading up to the attack, the duo had spent several weeks in Davao City in eastern Mindanao. While some investigative journalists suggested the journey was an attempt to establish ties with local jihadist networks, their precise motives for the trip remain unconfirmed. Crisis Group phone interviews, December 2025. Some locals fear that former militants could re-emerge. 11 Crisis Group interview, member of a peacebuilding non-governmental organisation from Maguindanao del Sur, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Remnants of the nationwide communist insurgency, the New People’s Army, also operate in parts of the region, particularly Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte. 12 Crisis Group Report N°338, Calming the Long War in the Philippine Countryside , 19 April 2024. According to government statistics, the insurgency numbers less than 1,000 fighters and no longer has any large units combining political cadres and fighters. Manila has looked to the military to patrol areas where these waning insurgencies persist. Meanwhile, the police take the lead in handling law and order in calmer areas, where guerrilla presence is negligible. Another obstacle to durable peace revolves around violent disputes over land and politics that have long plagued the region. Some of those are clan feuds, known as rido , and others are communal conflicts. These types of conflict are collectively referred to as “horizontal violence” by journalists and academics. 13 Crisis Group interview, civil society activist, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Clan feuds are comparable to vendettas. The number of shootings, particularly in Central Mindanao (Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Sur and parts of Lanao del Sur), is such that one parliamentarian described the atmosphere as “pervasive lawlessness”. 14 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 17 February 2026. A local conflict watchdog, using data from community networks, has recorded hundreds of incidents since January 2026 alone. See “Safeguard the Bangsamoro Vote: A critical period to transcend violence in the region”, Climate Conflict Action Asia, 30 July 2026. With many local disputes escalating into large-scale clashes, the failures of both the military and police to deter shootings have become conspicuous. The upcoming parliamentary elections are likely to aggravate tensions, as rival political blocs and local elites may enlist armed groups to intimidate voters or disturb the ballot. 15 Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro political strategist, 28 April 2026, Manila. The three local elections held in the region since its creation – in 2022, 2024 and 2025 – were less volatile than in the past but still featured high levels of violence. Infighting within the MILF is also a source of tension. 16 Crisis Group interviews, community leaders and officials, Cotabato City, 5-6 August 2026. While certain disputes stem from local resource control, deepening rifts within the MILF drive other conflicts. Frequently, these dynamics intertwine as factionalism amplifies existing land conflicts. Crisis Group interview, conflict researcher, Manila, 13 August 2026. Violence escalates quickly and frequently recurs in the region’s most conflict-affected areas, with outbreaks occurring most recently in the Special Geographic Area and parts of Maguindanao del Sur. 17 An ambush on Bangsamoro’s Chief Minister Macacua in the village of Bitu in Maguindanao del Norte by unidentified gunmen further highlighted the region’s volatility. The attack did not hurt anyone in Macacua’s convoy. Edwin Fernandez, “BARMM chief survives ambush in Maguindanao”, Inquirer , 16 August 2026. Criminal activity in the Bangsamoro also thrives wherever state authority is weak. While petty crimes such as theft or robberies are relatively rare in the region, illicit economies are ubiquitous, and have evolved in parallel to the peace process. 18 Crisis Group interviews, observers and police officers, February-March 2026. Kidnappings for ransom, which used to be Mindanao’s most lucrative business, have almost disappeared; smuggling, however, has proliferated, including for goods ranging from weapons to cooking oil. 19 Maritime Bangsamoro in particular, especially the provinces of Tawi-Tawi and Basilan, along with its former province Sulu, has traditionally been Mindanao’s “backdoor”, where many local communities have long treated smuggling to and from the Malaysian state of Sabah as legitimate commerce. In Central Mindanao, illicit cigarette trading has also flourished, much of it supplied from Indonesia and Vietnam and allegedly shielded by local powerbrokers. Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026; diplomats, Manila, 30 April 2026. See also, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, “ An Interconnected Criminal Ecosystem: Transnational Organized Crime Threat Assessment for South-East Asia ”, July 2026, pp. 216-217. This illicit activity, however, has not led to open violence between competing criminal interests as syndicates appear to work with local governments rather than against them, and turf wars are scarce. Human trafficking across the region, especially involving women, also remains a concern given the region’s porous borders and long coastlines. 20 See for example, Lean Bolongon, “Safeguarding minors: Combating illegal recruitment in BARMM”, Philippine Information Agency , 17 March 2026. Another profitable business in Mindanao is the drug trade. During former President Rodrigo Duterte’s term in office from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine police carried out a nation-wide anti-drug campaign that targeted suspected dealers and users, killing thousands. 21 Georgi Engelbrecht, “Philippines: The International Criminal Court Goes After Duterte’s Drug War”, 17 September 2021. While some Mindanao drug lords were killed, other networks survived and have since flourished. 22 Crisis Group interview, security analyst, Manila, 10 March 2026. As early as 2023 – just a year after Duterte left office – a local activist in Marawi declared that the “drugs are back”. 23 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 26 October 2023. The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and the police continue counter-narcotic operations; some locals say they have recently seen an increase in arrests and shoot-outs. 24 Crisis Group has recorded at least ten such anti-drug operations across the region in 2026 so far. One clash in August between security forces and an armed drug trafficking outfit in Bongao town in Tawi-Tawi left one person dead and three others wounded, including a naval officer. 25 Edwin Fernandez, “PDEA agent, drug suspect killed; 3 Marines wounded in Tawi-Tawi”, Inquirer , 9 August 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power. The proliferation of firearms has also contributed to conflict and crime in the region. 26 It is notoriously hard to determine the total number of guns in the region. In late 2024, the police estimated that the region had over 27,000 unregistered firearms, while a well-informed interlocutor told Crisis Group that there were 20,000 legally registered ones. Crisis Group interview, 11 February 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power; decades of war have made weapons ubiquitous. 27 Individuals and clans carry a wide variety of weapons, ranging from antiquated rifles to machine guns. Other Philippine regions where guns are prevalent are Abra and Negros. Members of armed groups and many local politicians, civilians and ex-combatants carry these weapons. 28 The first armed movement in the region, the MNLF, despite having splintered into factions, also retains weapons. The 1996 peace agreement with the movement sidestepped the question of disarmament, but in the absence of any attacks on government forces by a MNLF faction since 2012, Manila tolerates the awkward status quo of hundreds of MNLF fighters still being under arms. Crisis Group interviews, MNLF political cadre, Cotabato City, 16 February 2026. Under the 2014 peace agreement, the MILF has taken part in the gradual demobilisation of its forces. In early 2026, however, the group stopped formally participating in the process and other normalisation activities such high-level meetings due to Manila’s perceived failure to fulfil promises of socio-economic benefits for combatants who lay down their arms; 14,000 fighters have still to be decommissioned, along with 2,450 weapons. 29 Taher Solaiman, “MILF declares ‘temporary pause’ in peace process engagement with national government”, Luwaran.com , 17 March 2026. Following discussions between its peace panel and government counterparts, the MILF ended the temporary suspension of its engagement in the peace process in early August, but demobilisation of rebels appears to still be on hold. 30 Carolyn Arguillas, “GPH-MILF Peace Implementing Panels finally meet; MILF’s ‘temporary pause’ lifted”, Mindanews , 5 August 2026. While there has been a proliferation of Philippine gun laws over the past five decades, they are strikingly permissive. Under a so-called Type 5 licence, for example, Filipinos are allowed to possess up to fifteen firearms. Existing ordinances, moreover, are loosely enforced. Individuals often acquire weapons legally but then remove their serial numbers, making them untraceable. 31 Crisis Group interview, police officer, Manila, 10 May 2026. Consequently, the government’s main focus is on the pool of “loose” firearms – those guns which the state cannot trace or document – with the goal of either seizing them or persuading politicians and civilians to turn them in. 32 The term “loose firearms” refers broadly to weapons that rebels, criminals or civilians hold without proper registration, including those purchased legally but later left unregistered or with expired licenses. But the task is overwhelming; civil society activists say guns continue to flow in and out of the Bangsamoro without any means to trace them. 33 Crisis Group phone interview, source from Basilan, 28 February 2026. High-calibre weapons such as mortars, machine guns or assault rifles can easily stoke local conflicts as their lethality increases the likelihood of casualties and tit-for-tat retaliation. 34 On 2 August, national police chief Jose Nartatez pushed for a crackdown on illegal firearms and armed groups in the region ahead of the September polls. Andrea Gregorio, “PNP ramps up ops vs gun-for-hire groups ahead of BARMM polls”, Inquirer , 2 August 2026. For its part, the interim regional government has only recently started discussing a bill to regulate firearms and ammunition in the autonomous region. 35 Member of parliament Omar Sema filed the bill on 16 April 2026, marking the sole instance that such legislation has been discussed in the regional parliament, out of the 469 bills it has passed so far. In the meantime, local governments such as the province of Basilan have launched programs to collect small arms and light weapons. This effort is being done in coordination with the national peace process office and is underwritten by foreign donors. Buy-in, however, has been uneven. 36 An obstacle to these schemes is that the market value of firearms often surpasses the cash incentives offered to rebels or civilians for surrendering them. Two senior military commanders expressed deep scepticism about the campaign, arguing that the initiative would have no meaningful impact on the security landscape, was far too modest in scale, and targeted the wrong weapons (those not in the hands of rebels or ex-combatants). Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao and Cotabato, February-March 2026. Other proposed solutions, such as forced mass disarmament or the comprehensive registration of firearms, do not seem realistic in the Bangsamoro context. 37 Crisis Group interviews, interim government officials and civil society representatives, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Efforts to create “zones of peace” or “gun-free zones”, often initiated by non-government organisations, have been short-lived. 38 Crisis Group interview, head of a civil society organisation, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. Policing under Autonomy To meet the challenge of the post-conflict landscape, the drafters of the 2014 peace agreement had to think hard about the best way to police the region. 39 During the peace talks, policing was a key subject – as contentious as it was during negotiations between the government and the MNLF in 1996. That peace agreement contained no provisions for disarmament or demobilisation, and clashes continued to flare more than a decade after the deal. While the 1996 agreement envisaged integrating MNLF rebels into state forces, only a quarter of the insurgent force eventually joined the police or military, voluntarily bringing with them more than 4,000 firearms Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 26 February 2026. See also, Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, “Integration of MNLF forces into the PNP and AFP: Integration without demobilization and disarmament”, unpublished paper for UP Center on Integrative and Development Studies project on the GRP-MNLF peace agreement, 2000. The agreement called for a regional police force that was to be “civilian in character, effective and efficient in law enforcement, fair and impartial, and accountable under the law for its actions”, and whose mandate would be “law enforcement and maintenance of peace and order” in the region. 40 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro and Annex on Normalisation . But the division of labour between Manila, its national police force and the region remained ambiguous. 41 The Philippine National Police, created in 1991, is tasked with preventing and investigating criminal activities and strengthening internal security. The Department of Interior and Local Government has political control over the force, while the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) administers and disciplines it. The president selects the national police chief and senior police officers and appoints the secretary of the department of interior and local government. Headquartered in Manila, the force maintains regional, provincial and municipal stations across the archipelago, but also includes two specialised units: the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group focuses on organised crime and terrorism; the Special Action Force, the PNP’s elite commando unit, is in charge of counterterrorism, hostage rescue, and high-risk operations as well as ad hoc tasks such as patrolling hot spots during elections. One part of the agreement stipulated that the regional government, working in coordination with Manila, “shall have primary responsibility over public order and safety within the Bangsamoro”. 42 Annex on Power Sharing , Art. II, 14. In another part, the accord said the police force is “responsible both to the central government and the Bangsamoro government”. 43 Framework Agreement and Annex on Normalisation. The Philippine Constitution is clear in that regard, as Art. 10 Section 21 states: “The preservation of peace and order within the regions shall be the responsibility of the local police agencies which shall be organised, maintained, supervised, and utilised in accordance with applicable laws. The defence and security of the regions shall be the responsibility of the National Government”. Government officials involved in the negotiations say the agreement was clear the regional police would remain under national authority. 44 One official involved in the process, however, said that Manila dodged the hard questions until the end, keeping the wording intentionally vague, and ended up “parking” the issue for the future. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 31 July 2026. The MILF, however, maintains that the common understanding in talks was that policing should be under the control of the autonomous government. The agreement also set up an Independent Commission on Policing to determine how law enforcement should function in the new region. When the commission delivered its report in April 2014, it recommended that the force remain a part of the national police, but stressed that it should invest in community‑based policing. 45 The Independent Commission on Policing for the Bangsamoro, “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, 2014. Report on file with Crisis Group. Community policing is generally understood as an approach that builds active partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to solve community problems and jointly ensure public safety. The commission highlighted the need for community policing that respects human rights and Sharia law. Another problem the commission identified was the police’s weak accountability to the communities they serve. Tasked with translating the occasionally vague peace agreement into clear and legally binding terms, the 2019 autonomy law dismissed the idea of a separate Bangsamoro police force. Wary of clashing with the 1987 constitution’s centralised approach to policing, lawmakers assigned public order and safety to the national government. 46 A single national police force was mandated to curb the historical misuse of local law enforcement by warlords. Yet mindful of the authoritarian practices during Martial Law under Ferdinand Marcos, the constitution balanced this by granting local governments a supervisory role to ensure checks and balances. This outcome reflected the stance of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who was in office when the autonomy law came into force, but both the national police force and lawyers were also sceptical about proposals for a separate regional police force. 47 Crisis Group telephone interview, analyst, 18 February 2021. In early 2019, the national police established a Police Regional Office (PRO-BARMM), which is part of the national police and therefore firmly under Manila’s control. 48 According to most observers and local figures, any change to this status quo needs constitutional amendments. Crisis Group written communication, 12 June 2026. See also, Nash Maulana, “‘BARMM police, Moro Senate seat require Charter change”, Manila Standard , 3 May 2026. At the same time, the organic law included two compromise provisions. The first one was to allow the integration of MILF and MNLF members into PRO-BARMM (see Section III.A.2). 49 The MILF was critical towards integration of their forces into the police during the peace talks. Later, however, the movement accepted this provision in the autonomy law. The second one called for the chief of the regional police force to be appointed “upon consultation with the Chief Minister”. In practice, however, it is the national police chief who has ultimately decided on this appointment. 50 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. In late 2025, however, a national police commission resolution reiterated that the region’s chief minister can both recommend candidates and provide feedback on shortlisted officers. III. Security and Justice in Transition Various bodies in the Bangsamoro region are responsible for tackling flare-ups of violence. While the police and military remain central to maintaining order, other government and community institutions also help dispense justice and mediate disputes. A. The Police during the Bangsamoro Transition As is the case with the national police as a whole, the Bangsamoro force is hierarchical in nature. Its regional headquarters are in Parang, from which it oversees five provincial headquarters and more than one hundred municipal police stations. Every town has a team of officers who mostly take care of basic law enforcement. These tasks include investigating crimes, preparing requests for warrants or subpoenas from the courts, dealing with minor offences and arresting criminals and insurgents. 51 Arrest powers remain outside the military’s purview, except in instances of “in flagrante delicto” where troops directly witness a crime. The number of officers in the region is, by many accounts, insufficient: a regular station typically has a staff of a bit over twenty, covering municipalities with populations as large as 25,000. Overall, the police force’s headcount stands at over 7,000. 52 Crisis Group interviews, police officers, Cotabato City and Parang, 6-7 August 2026. Every municipal police chief shapes the local force’s policies on everything from community engagement and collaboration with politicians to defining how to handle local conflicts. In the post-2019 transition period, the police has emphasised anti-drug operations and curbing the spread of illegal firearms. 53 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. These priorities stem from the national government’s priority of combating drugs, as well as community support for the campaign. 54 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Cotabato City, 6 August 2026. Given their limited numbers and lack of equipment, it has been more difficult for the police to address complex clan feuds, which can flare up without forewarning. In the most conflict-affected parts of Maguindanao, the police struggle to conduct even routine patrols, leaving law and order in the military’s hands. 55 A police chief from the region distinguished between “law enforcement”, for which the police is in the lead, and “combat operations” that are the domain of the military. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 17 February 2026. A senior police officer said the force can take care of so-called “soft targets”, but still need back-up if the operation occurs in a “harsh” context. 56 Crisis Group interview, Shariff Aguak, Maguindanao del Sur, 27 March 2026. According to one regional bureaucrat, the police may be willing to take over internal security but is currently “not capable” of doing so. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Perceptions of law enforcers vary. The police appear more connected to everyday life than the military because their stations are located near town halls, making them visibly present. Some officers have a genuine desire to help their communities. But for many young Moro men and women, becoming a police officer is more about acquiring a secure job than answering the call of duty. 57 Crisis Group interview, member of parliament, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 13 February 2026; academic, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Some locals are also sceptical about the ability of the police to respond to incidents. 58 In Lanao del Sur, a civil society activist also observed the police are too slow to respond to violence. Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Locals in predominantly non-Moro Indigenous communities also feel that law enforcement does not always respond to their concerns. 59 Crisis Group interview, phone interview, community leader, 6 December 2021; online communication, peace process observer, 17 August 2026. That said, several surveys show the police enjoy a degree of trust from local people. 60 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 20 March 2026. Surveys made available to Crisis Group. Other survey data suggests that many residents continue to look to local leaders and religious figures for security. Tatsuya Koyama, “Who Supports the Peace? A Survey of Postconflict Public Opinion in Maguindanao, the Philippines”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 44 no. 3 (December 2025). At the beginning of the transition, many MILF commanders hoped community policing – namely, building partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to ensure public safety – would become widespread. 61 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Cotabato City, 27 November 2019. The Philippine police have used civilian auxiliaries known as the Barangay Peace Action Teams (BPATs) and Civilian Volunteer Organisations (CVOs) that came closest to community policing. With police approval, BPATs may carry light firearms. CVOs focus on intelligence gathering, neighbourhood patrols, and emergency response. Officially unarmed, they may use weapons when supporting police operations, although in practice some mayors or village heads have been known to issue them firearms. Despite the support of international donors, however, and its inclusion in the Philippine policing doctrine, this approach never really gained momentum. 62 Crisis Group interview, donor official, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Police officers admit that resource limitations, understaffing and local politics complicate the work of fostering stronger relations with Bangsamoro communities. 63 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato and Parang, 5-7 August 2026. Even so, some individual officers have been more proactive. A former police chief in Maguindanao, for example, instructed his officers to visit communities and engage residents on important concerns, at times accompanied by representatives from the judicial system. 64 This community outreach mostly relates to drugs and firearms use. Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. As for efforts to integrate MILF fighters into the police force, as stipulated in the autonomy law (see Section II.B), these have so far had limited success. In 2019, the government waived height, age, and education requirements for five years to allow more former MILF (and MNLF) rebels to qualify for recruitment in the regional force. After a two-year interruption due to the COVID-19 pandemic, 11,075 applicants took a special eligibility exam in May 2022, which 7,145 passed. Yet in the years that followed, the government earmarked only about 400 positions for the former fighters, and just 396 joined the police force. 65 At present, 36 women were considered for recruitment and have undergone on-the-job-training in police stations across the region. “The Peace Accords Matrix – Mindanao (PAM-M) and Civil Society Normalization Update Report (January-April 2026)”, University of Notre Dame, 3 August 2026, p. 11. While the interim government stepped in to fund their training, Manila subsequently grew sceptical of maintaining dedicated quotas for ex-rebels, and future applicants will have to compete within the general pool of all Filipinos vying for the 1,500 police positions available annually. 66 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. A small concession was a resolution by the national police commission in July 2025, which extended the police application deadline for MILF and MNLF members to 8 June 2027. Bong Sarmiento, “MILF, MNLF members who want to become cops can apply until June 2027”, Inquirer , 17 July 2025. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. 67 Crisis Group interview, Manila, international observer, 21 October 2022. Police officers from Cotabato City said MILF recruits have been well‑received by their new colleagues, and a sense of camaraderie now animates the ranks. 68 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 28 March 2026, 6 August 2026. The Third Party Monitoring Team – an independent body mandated with overseeing the peace process – has encouraged further recruitment, underlining it “could serve as a powerful symbol of previously warring entities working constructively to build a secure future together”. 69 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. But prospects for further integration appear dim. Manila has demonstrated no appetite to reintroduce a quota for ex-rebels or hire Moro who passed the exam but were not incorporated into the force. A part of the MILF, furthermore, still expects the regional government to take over policing in the region in the long term. 70 Crisis Group interview, international observer, Manila, 14 October 2022. Crisis Group interviews, MILF officials, February-March 2026. In this sense, the policing issue is emblematic of a broader lack of agreement on the future of the peace process. 71 Crisis Group interviews, international and local observers, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. Marking its new secretary’s first 100 days, the Philippine peace process office’s late-July report made no mention of policing.
